rows.body:
Consider the following simplified code:

template <class T> class Foo {
    T t;
    const T* t_ptr;
public:
    constexpr Foo(T t): t(t), t_ptr(&this->t) {}
    constexpr Foo(const Foo& foo): t(foo.t), t_ptr(&this->t) {}
    constexpr T get_t() const {
        return *t_ptr;
    }
};
template <class T> constexpr Foo<T> foo(T t) {
    return Foo<T>(t);
}

constexpr auto f = foo(1);
static_assert(f.get_t() == 1);

It successfully compiles with Clang and MSVC but GCC 15 reports an error:

<source>:16:25: error: non-constant condition for static assertion
   16 | static_assert(f.get_t() == 1);
      |               ~~~~~~~~~~^~~~
<source>:16:22:   in 'constexpr' expansion of 'f.Foo<int>::get_t()'
<source>:8:17: error: the value of 'f' is not usable in a constant expression
    8 |         return *t_ptr;
      |                 ^~~~~
<source>:15:16: note: 'f' used in its own initializer
   15 | constexpr auto f = foo(1);
      |                ^
Compiler returned: 1

Is this code valid? Is this a bug in GCC? Is there a workaround to make constexpr structs that contain a pointer to its own member work?
rows.key_body:
I think it is a gcc bug.

Some variants pass when calling constructors directly Demo

I think gcc badly implements the note from copy_elision (code "similar" to yours).

In constant expression and constant initialization, copy elision is never performed.
rows.title: constexpr self-referencing struct

rows.body:
I've done an experimental program able to handle speed, length, time, their units of measure and do few calculations with them (here, in fr.sympathique.explicite package, and here for the tests).

It gives average speeds in km/h from various length and time units.

// Runner A : 1.6 km in 4 minutes
Speed averageSpeedA = new Speed(1.6, KILOMETRE, 4.0, MINUTE);
averageSpeedA.convert(HOUR);

LOGGER.info("Runner A : {}", averageSpeedA); // 24 km/h
assertEquals(24.0, averageSpeedA.speed(), 0.001);

// Marathonian B : 42 km in 2.25 h
Length distanceB = new Length(KILOMETRE, 42.0);
Speed averageSpeedB = new Speed(distanceB.length(), KILOMETRE, 2.25, HOUR);

LOGGER.info("Marathonian B : {}", averageSpeedB); // 18.667 km/h
assertEquals(18.666, averageSpeedB.speed(), 0.001);

But I'd like this program being written like:

Speed averageSpeedA = 1.6 km / 4.0 min;
averageSpeedA.convert(HOUR);

Length distanceB = 42.0 km;
Speed averageSpeedB = distanceB / 2.25 h;

(units of measure symbols are expected sufficient (for a while at least) to discriminate enough the type of object requested to carry a value)

This I guess I can perform with the help of:

  1. Creating a specific Compiler Plugin, such as shown here.

  2. Generate a part of Java code to compile, handling operators and units of measure with AntLR.

Is that theoretically possible, reachable with some work, or is this a false trail?
rows.key_body:
Frankly: no.

And now for the context: if this is just a fun programming exercise, by all means go ahead and do it.

If you really want to release this into the wild, practically nobody will be willing to augment his build with a compiler plugin just for conversion of measurements. The problem is too small and the solution too big to find a real user base.

If you really really want to create a custom language (which I absolutely understand, because it is plain FUN), my advice would be to create an interpreter using antlr, which can interpret a text block:

  Speed = mycustomthingy.evaluate("""  
      Distance distance = 42.0 km;
      return distance / 2.5h;
  """);

(I can't seem to shake off java-syntax - feel free to design whatever you feel like ;-))
rows.title: Do you think that creating a Java Compiler Plugin and using AntLR to handle operations on values having units of measure could be a correct choice?

rows.body:
What does constexpr void wait(T old, /*...*/) const noexcept; do during constant evaluation, now that it's constexpr in C++26?

The description says that it in a loop:

Blocks until it is unblocked by an atomic notifying operation or is unblocked spuriously.

But since there is no multithreading at compile time, it seems like blocking the main thread means deadlocking the compiler.
rows.key_body:
This is explained in the proposal

Wait and notify operations should work during constant evaluation as expected in a single-threaded environment. Notify will be noop and wait-ing for a different value will be a deadlock which should result in constant evaluation failure according to [expr.const#5.7] an expression that would exceed the implementation-defined limits as every check for the value is considered [intro.progress#4] continous executing of execution steps while waiting for the condition.
rows.title: What does constexpr atomic<T>::wait() do at compile time?

rows.body:
I'm wondering why std::string can't be constexpr if it's a stack variable:

#include <string>
#include <iostream>
#include <cstring>

constexpr std::string str15 {"123456789012345"}; // This compiles!

struct Foo
{
    constexpr Foo() : a(6) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i)
            buff[i] = 0;
    }
    int a;
    char buff[8];
};

constexpr void func()
{
    constexpr Foo f{}; // This compiles
    constexpr std::string str15 {"123456789012345"}; // This doesn't compile
}

int main() {
    func();
    return 0;
}

Error:

'std::string{std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>::_Alloc_hider{((char*)(& str15.std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>::<anonymous>.std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>::<unnamed union>::_M_local_buf))}, 15, std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>::<unnamed union>{char [16]{'1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7', '8', '9', '0', '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', 0}}}' is not a constant expression

I get the stack variable and the static variable are different places in memory, but the compiler will accept arbitrary objects as local variables as constexpr. My Foo class doesn't have a const char* as argument, so that's a difference, but it's not as if const char* constructor can't be used in constexpr, because higher above:

constexpr std::string str15 {"123456789012345"}; // This compiles

https://godbolt.org/z/cffPq6nns
rows.key_body:
The difference between your class Foo and std::basic_string boils down to libstdc++ implementation of SSO, where the latter has a member of pointer type, which uses the underlying data array as initializer.

This in turn violates possible values a pointer can take in a constant expression (provided the enclosing object doesn't have static storage duration). From cppreference.com:

If the value is of pointer type, it is one of the following values:

  • the address of an object with static storage duration
  • the address past the end of an object with static storage duration
  • the address of a (non-immediate(since C++20)) function
  • a null pointer value

If Foo had such a pointer, it would suffer from the same problem:

struct Foo
{
    char buff[8];
    char* ptr = buff;
};

int main() {
    constexpr Foo f{}; // Doesn't compile
    return 0;
}
rows.title: Why can std::string create a constexpr object only if it's a static variable?

rows.body:
I wonder whether this piece of code should compile and what function it should call. The situation is that there is a struct whose name matches that of a template parameter. My question is, inside the definition of the f<U> specialization (where U derives from T), does T mean the template parameter or the base class?

template<typename T> 
void f(T t) {
    t.T::~T(); // #1 should this compile?
    t.T::m(); // #2 should this compile? 
}

struct T { ~T() {} void m(){}}; // note named like the typename parameter
struct U : private T { ~U() {} void m(){}}; // note inherits from T

int main()
{
    f(U{});
}

Well, from naive look, it should compile #1 and #2, and find U::m(), and call the destructor of U;

But, I tried it on compilers using Godbolt https://godbolt.org/z/3KG8M5xvb and the behavior is not as I thought.

On Clang, it calls the destructor of U but it tries to call the base member function ::T::m() instead of ::U::m() leading to a compile error on #2.

On GCC, it calls the destructor of the base class U and the member function ::U::m() no compiler errors which matches my expectations.

MSVC raises errors on both lines saying it cannot access private base ::T destructor and private member function ::T::f().

Which compiler is correct, or is this implementation defined behavior?

I tried to read the standard to determine the answer but I don't understand it.
rows.key_body:
The lookup for T in T:: is defined as happening in the class first and as an unqualified lookup only if that finds nothing ([basic.lookup.qual.general]/3). That rule is, however, quite unsatisfying in cases like this: a template that works with types derived from one of its template parameters has no way of referring to that base class in a way that avoids collisions with members of the same name in the derived class. (A non-template could always use a fully qualified name for the base class.)

This has been the subject of a core issue for a long time, and I tried to change the rule, but it was CWG’s opinion that the adjacent . (or ->) was just too important to look past (even only for dependent names).

The situation with ~T is even weirder, just because destructor “names” can successfully refer only to the type of the object expression or the nested name specifier. Here both qualified and unqualified lookup occur, but all that matters is that at least one matches that type, and obviously the qualified one will be the same as for T::.
rows.title: typename in qualified member access

However, when I try to import the LangChain library into my project, I keep receiving the same error repeatedly:

Here is my import code:

rows.key_body:
langchain==1.0.5

langchain v1.0 was released recently (October 22, 2025), and according to the release notes, .chains and .retrievers have been moved to the langchain-classic package:

# Chains
from langchain_classic.chains import ...

# Retrievers
from langchain_classic.retrievers import ...

You're getting a ModuleNotFoundError because those imports do not exist in the langchain package in v1.0. That's why I asked for your version numbers in Staging Ground.

Some usage can be migrated to the new API; for RAG, you can look at the current RAG docs. The specific migration path depends on exactly what you were trying to do, which may be the subject of a separate question.

You can also temporarily downgrade back to v0.3 to use the older API, but it is in "maintenance" mode and will only continue to receive limited support ("security patches and critical bug fixes") until December 2026.

rows.body:
I've been using Tailwind CSS for my projects for a long time. Starting my new project, I installed the package and created the tailwind.config.js file via the command npx tailwindcss init -p, as I'm used to. But then I ran into an unexpected error – npm can't find the executable called by npx tailwindcss, even though I installed it.

Reproducing the error message is as simple as running the following two commands from the root of the project :

$ npm install -D tailwindcss
$ npx tailwindcss init -p

  npm error could not determine executable to run
  npm error A complete log of this run can be found in:
  ...

Why am I running into this error when it used to work before?
rows.key_body:
TL;DR (for init process): Since v4, there is no need for a tailwind.config.js file, so the init process is also unnecessary, making both outdated. Review the v4 installation guides, where the init step is not included. Or install v3 with specifically changed guide.

TL;DR (for Tailwind CLI): Previous content + In v4, Tailwind CLI was separated from the core package, so an additional package needs to be installed see below and in How to use Tailwind CLI.

TailwindCSS v4

TailwindCSS has just released its new v4 version, so all the older v3 documentation has become somewhat outdated.

  • Upgrade guide - TailwindCSS v3 to v4

Changed npx tailwindcss to npx @tailwindcss/cli

The command to run is now no longer npx tailwindcss but npx @tailwindcss/cli.

PostCSS plugin and CLI are separate packages — the main tailwindcss package doesn't include these anymore since not everyone needs them, instead they should be installed separately using @tailwindcss/postcss and @tailwindcss/cli.

Source: Open-sourcing our progress on Tailwind CSS v4.0 - Whats changed

This is basically only necessary if you're not using it with a framework and want to run it from the command line. For this, a standalone @tailwindcss/cli package will help from v4 onwards.

npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/cli
  • Get started with Tailwind CSS - TailwindCSS v4 Docs
  • TailwindCSS v4 Alpha: Using the CLI

Deprecated init process

In v4, the installation process has changed. It's now simpler. The init command has become obsolete and is no longer usable from v4 onwards because it's not needed anymore.

  • tailwindlabs/tailwindcss #15791 - init process not available - GitHub

Using the upgrade tool

If you'd like to try upgrading a project from v3 to v4, you can use our upgrade tool to do the vast majority of the heavy lifting for you:

npx @tailwindcss/upgrade@next
  • How to using the upgrade tool - Tailwind CSS v4 Docs
  • Unable to upgrade Tailwind CSS v3 to v4 - Related: an interesting fact about this

Other related changes from v4

  • Removed @tailwind directives
  • Deprecated: Sass, Less and Stylus preprocessors support
  • @import "tailwindcss"; does not work when used in a file with an .scss extension
  • Automatic Source Detection from TailwindCSS v4
  • Adding an external source or a package from within node_modules for detection
  • [postcss] It looks like you're trying to use tailwindcss directly as a PostCSS plugin

TailwindCSS v3

For a installation, you'll already be installing v4. However, if you want to install v3, use the old documentation with the following command:

npm install tailwindcss@3
  • Get started - TailwindCSS v3 Docs
  • Cannot build frontend using Vite, TailwindCSS with PostCSS - StackOverflow
rows.title: Tailwind CSS: "npm error could not determine executable to run"

rows.key_body:
TLDR for those who came here looking for clues when facing Bochs' log like fetch_raw_descriptor: GDT: index (ff57) 1fea > limit (2f):

Start Bochs with the debugger enabled, execute show int & show dbg_all in the Bochs debugger CLI, and then run your image. This would make Bochs to log all interrupts/exceptions; if this error occurred during interrupt handling, you'll get some more clues into what was happening.

Now, to the question. First let's see the logs.

19849108391e[CPU0  ] fetch_raw_descriptor: GDT: index (ff57) 1fea > limit (2f)
19849108391e[CPU0  ] interrupt(): gate descriptor is not valid sys seg (vector=0x08)

Vector 0x08 is a double fault vector. So presumably there was some exception, and the attempt to process it resulted in a double fault. Moreover, the attempt to process a double fault also resulted in a fault, presumably because the trap segments value in IDT was not a valid system segment. Something is wrong in your IDT; and also there was that first exception, so something is wrong there too.

19849108391i[CPU0  ] | EAX=00100023...
19849108391i[CPU0  ] | ESP=00800000...
19849108391i[CPU0  ] | SEG sltr(index|ti|rpl)     base    limit G D
19849108391i[CPU0  ] |  CS:001b( 0003| 0|  3) 00000000 ffffffff 1 1
19849108391i[CPU0  ] |  DS:0023( 0004| 0|  3) 00000000 ffffffff 1 1
19849108391i[CPU0  ] |  SS:0023( 0004| 0|  3) 00000000 ffffffff 1 1
19849108391i[CPU0  ] | EIP=00100023 (00100023)
19849108391i[CPU0  ] | CR2=0x00100023
19849108391i[CPU0  ] 0x0000000000100023>> or byte ptr ds:[esi-117], ah : 08668B

Ok, so the exception happens upon jump to User mode. CS is 0x1B as expected, and the rest of the segments are 0x23 as expected. ESP is 0x800000 as expected. It seems the cross-privilege level iret did its job. The segment shadow contents looks fine as well.

EIP looks wrong however. It points into the kernel, somewhere in the middle of an instruction. CR2 is the same as EIP which suggests the initial exception was a paging exception; CPU couldn't read the code instruction (which is expected I guess if the kernel pages are set as system). EAX is the same as EIP (and it holds the initial EIP value in enter_user_mode, so probably the very first instruction faulted).

19849108391e[CPU0  ] exception(): 3rd (13) exception with no resolution, shutdown status is 00h, resetting

This is the triple-fault reset, because a double-fault could not be processed.

Ok, so 1) exception handling doesn't work, and it should(?) and 2) a bad EIP.

That 0x23 in the end of EIP is highly suspect, because it matches the data segment value. Surely enough, enter_user_mode is buggy:

  00100b10 <enter_user_mode>:
  100b10:       fa                      cli
  100b11:       8b 44 24 04             mov    0x4(%esp),%eax
  100b15:       66 b8 23 00             mov    $0x23,%ax

EIP value gets loaded into eax, but then ax is also loaded with 0x23 which destroys half of the value. Fix is trivial: simply use different registers; e.g. use 'dx' for the selector value.

With that fixed, we get

19960859176i[CPU0  ] | EIP=00108000 (00108000)
19960859176i[CPU0  ] | CR2=0x00108000
19960859176i[CPU0  ] 0x0000000000108000>> mov eax, 0xdeadbeef : B8EFBEADDE

Ok, so now it faults at the actual usermode start. Why does it do that? Well, because it’s still a system-mode page. There is nothing in your code to prepare the actual user-mode region of virtual addresses. From the book (para 11.2):

There are a few things every user mode process needs: Page frames for code, data and stack. At the moment it suffices to allocate one page frame for the stack and enough page frames to fit the program’s code. Don’t worry about setting up a stack that can be grow and shrink at this point in time, focus on getting a basic implementation work first. The binary from the GRUB module has to be copied to the page frames used for the programs code. A page directory and page tables are needed to map the page frames described above into memory. At least two page tables are needed, because the code and data should be mapped in at 0x00000000 and increasing, and the stack should start just below the kernel, at 0xBFFFFFFB, growing towards lower addresses. The U/S flag has to be set to allow PL3 access.

None of that has been done. There isn’t any stack space allocated, and there aren’t any user-mode pages to hold the user-space code. This fault is expected; the kernel just isn't ready to run userspace.

Ok, with that figured out, let's return to the IDT handling. Looking at interrupts_install_idt, it is immediately obvious that it could use some love. At least the internal exceptions handlers should be all filled up (also note exception 7 is not error-code bearing; the list of such exceptions is provided in the book). It would be a good idea to add some handling of the exceptions also; one common approach is to log an exception, CPU, state, etc. Well, see the Bochs log for an example. Your code could do something similar.

I have to say the book has dropped the ball here. This is a tricky subject, and the book gives two rough examples of C side (paragraph 6.3) and assembly side (paragraph 6.4) of interrupt handler, but they are not compatible with each other! interrupt_handler has to be called according to its declaration (or vice versa); kudos to you for fixing that (I am not sure if struct ordering is correct though).

All that said, the code does look fine at first glance. It should've been a page fault, which should've been handled at least somehow. Moreover, Bochs debugger can show IDT contents, and it's fine; the segment values are correct. Let's switch Bochs' debugging logs on and see what's happening in more details ("show int", "show dbg_all" in the Bochs debugger CLI):

CPU 0: Exception 0x0e - (#PF) page fault occurred (error_code=0x0005)
CPU 0: Interrupt 0x0e occurred (error_code=0x0005)
07358149912e[CPU0  ] fetch_raw_descriptor: GDT: index (ff57) 1fea > limit (2f)
CPU 0: Exception 0x0a - (#TS) invalid TSS occurred (error_code=0xff51)
CPU 0: Exception 0x08 - (#DF) double fault occurred (error_code=0x0000)
CPU 0: Interrupt 0x08 occurred (error_code=0x0000)
07358149912e[CPU0  ] fetch_raw_descriptor: GDT: index (ff57) 1fea > limit (2f)
CPU 0: Exception 0x0a - (#TS) invalid TSS occurred (error_code=0xff51)

Ah yes, IDT itself is not an issue. Here we have a cross-privilege trap (switching from user-mode at ring 3 to kernel at ring 0). That involves switching the stack, and switching the stack needs TSS (so the CPU has a place to store ring 3 SS/ESP and load ring 0 SS/ESP). There isn’t any TSS set in the code, and therefore any exceptions in ring 3 would result in a crash. Well, the book hints at such problems in paragraph 11.3:

For now, we should have interrupts disabled, as it requires a little more work to get inter-privilege level interrupts to work properly (see the section “System calls”).

And indeed, later on in section "system calls" (paragraph 13.2), it talks about setting up TSS and why it is needed. Without that done, you have to rely on Bochs' debugger and logs to deal with any bugs.
rows.title: Why is my kernel logging an exception and interrupt when I run it, attempting to enter user mode?

rows.body:
My custom OAuth2AuthorizationFailureHandler can load the current cached token, but I need the token used by the request that failed so that invalidation does not remove its replacement. These can differ when a replacement is stored while a request is in flight.

In a non-servlet client_credentials application, concurrent callers share an OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor, a client registration and a principal. The ordering I need to handle is:

  1. A resource request is sent with T1.
  2. Another caller stores T2 for the same registration/principal while that request is in flight.
  3. The request using T1 receives 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token".

I tried a custom handler that loads the OAuth2AuthorizedClient from the service. This deterministic example shows its inputs; the handler only logs them and does not remove anything. The execution stub models step 2 before returning the 401, without threads or external servers.

Tested with Java 21, Spring Security 7.1.1 and Spring Framework 7.0.9. Dependencies: spring-security-oauth2-client:7.1.1, spring-web:7.0.9, spring-test:7.0.9, jakarta.servlet-api:6.1.0 and their transitive dependencies.

import java.net.URI;
import java.time.Instant;

import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.mock.http.client.MockClientHttpRequest;
import org.springframework.mock.http.client.MockClientHttpResponse;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.TestingAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.*;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.registration.*;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.web.client.OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.*;

public class Late401CustomHandler {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var registration = ClientRegistration.withRegistrationId("demo")
                .clientId("demo").clientSecret("unused")
                .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.CLIENT_CREDENTIALS)
                .tokenUri("https://issuer.invalid/token").build();
        Authentication principal = new TestingAuthenticationToken("service", "unused");
        var service = new InMemoryOAuth2AuthorizedClientService(
                new InMemoryClientRegistrationRepository(registration));
        service.saveAuthorizedClient(client(registration, "T1"), principal);

        // Use the cached client so the example needs no token endpoint.
        OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager = request ->
                service.loadAuthorizedClient("demo", principal.getName());
        var interceptor = new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(manager);
        interceptor.setClientRegistrationIdResolver(request -> "demo");
        interceptor.setPrincipalResolver(request -> principal);
        interceptor.setAuthorizationFailureHandler((error, authentication, attributes) -> {
            OAuth2AuthorizedClient current =
                    service.loadAuthorizedClient("demo", authentication.getName());
            System.out.println("failure=" + error.getError().getErrorCode());
            System.out.println("cached=" + current.getAccessToken().getTokenValue());
            System.out.println("attributeKeys=" + attributes.keySet());
        });

        var request = new MockClientHttpRequest(HttpMethod.GET,
                URI.create("https://resource.invalid/data"));
        interceptor.intercept(request, new byte[0], (sent, body) -> {
            System.out.println("sent=" + sent.getHeaders().getFirst(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION));
            // Model another caller storing T2 while the request using T1 is in flight.
            service.saveAuthorizedClient(client(registration, "T2"), principal);
            var response = new MockClientHttpResponse(new byte[0], HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
            response.getHeaders().set(HttpHeaders.WWW_AUTHENTICATE,
                    "Bearer error=\"invalid_token\"");
            return response;
        }).close();
    }

    private static OAuth2AuthorizedClient client(ClientRegistration registration, String token) {
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        return new OAuth2AuthorizedClient(registration, "service",
                new OAuth2AccessToken(OAuth2AccessToken.TokenType.BEARER,
                        token, now.minusSeconds(1), now.plusSeconds(3600)));
    }
}

Output:

sent=Bearer T1
failure=invalid_token
cached=T2
attributeKeys=[]

Reading the authorized client inside the handler therefore gives me T2, not the token T1 used by the failed request. In the 7.1.1 interceptor source, handleAuthorizationFailure creates a new attributes map and adds servlet request/response objects only when a servlet request context exists. In this non-servlet example the map is empty.

How should I carry the failed request's bearer token into the failure callback so the store can atomically remove only the matching token? A wrapper or another extension point is acceptable. I want to preserve invalidation when the cached token matches the failed request, while retaining T2 when a late failure belongs to T1, without serializing complete resource requests.
rows.key_body:
OAuth2AuthorizationFailureHandler doesn't get the OAuth2AuthorizedClient or the access token from the failed request. Rereading the client within the handler is a risky operation since some other request might have already replaced T1 with T2.

Thus, the approach is to retrieve the bearer token from the HTTP request and conditionally invalidate the token currently in use.

It can be done via wrapper for OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor.

But one thing to note here: the wrapper should listen to the Authorization header after Spring Security has populated it with the token.

If you are dealing with Spring ClientHttpRequestInterceptor then it can be done by wrapping ClientHttpRequestExecution which is provided to OAuth2 interceptor

ClientHttpRequestInterceptor captureToken =
        (request, body, execution) -> {

    ClientHttpRequestExecution wrappedExecution = (sent, sentBody) -> {
        String authorization =
                sent.getHeaders().getFirst(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION);

        String failedToken = null;

        if (authorization != null && authorization.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
            failedToken = authorization.substring(7);
        }

        ClientHttpResponse response = execution.execute(sent, sentBody);

        if (response.getStatusCode().value() == 401
                && isInvalidToken(response)
                && failedToken != null) {

            removeIfTokenMatches(
                    "demo",
                    "service",
                    failedToken
            );
        }

        return response;
    };

    return interceptor.intercept(request, body, wrappedExecution);
};
rows.title: How can a Spring Security OAuth2 failure handler access the token used by the failed request?

rows.body:
Consider this example:

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>

int main(){
  std::atomic<int> epoch = {0};
  std::atomic<int> value = {1};
  std::jthread t1([&](){
     epoch.store(1,std::memory_order::seq_cst);  // #1
     value.load(std::memory_order::seq_cst);  // #2
  });
  
  std::jthread t2([&](){
     value.exchange(2,std::memory_order::seq_cst); // #3
     epoch.load(std::memory_order::seq_cst); // #4
  });
}

In this example, if #2 read 1, then #4 must read #1, because it's guaranteed by the single total order #1 < #2 < #3 < #4. For other cases, #4 can either read the initial value or #1, they correspond to a valid single total order #3 < #4 < #1 < #2, or #3 < #1 < #2 < #4(or, #3 < #1 < #4 < #2), respectively.

If change the example to the following:

#include <atomic>
#include <thread>

int main(){
  std::atomic<int> epoch = {0};
  std::atomic<int> value = {1};
  std::jthread t1([&](){
     epoch.store(1,std::memory_order::relaxed);  // #1
     value.fetch_add(0,std::memory_order::acq_rel);  // #2
  });
  
  std::jthread t2([&](){
     value.exchange(2,std::memory_order::acq_rel); // #3
     epoch.load(std::memory_order::relaxed); // #4
  });
}

In this example, if #2 read 1, according to [atomics.order] p10

Atomic read-modify-write operations shall always read the last value (in the modification order) written before the write associated with the read-modify-write operation.

#3 must follow #2 in the modification order of value. Because their memory orders are acq_rel, #2 must happens-before #3, so the visibility of #1 to #4 is now guaranteed by the happens-before. Similarly, for other cases, #4 can either read 0 or #1. IIUC, these two programs are functionally equivalent in observable behaviors.

This first snippet of code is simplified from the EBR algorithm(i.e., Epoch-Based Reclamation). #3 emulates the operation that updates the pointer, the core idea is that, if #2 reads the old pointer value, it must precede #3 in the single total order, so #1 also precedes #4 in the single total order; therefore, #4 must see #1 to check whether the reader's epoch is the current one.

If we only consider the correctness of implementing the core idea(i.e., the EBR algorithm), can I change the memory order seq_cst to acq_rel by changing the corresponding operations to those in the second example? IIUC, they should have the same correctness; merely, the visibility of #1 is guaranteed by the single total order in the first way, and is guaranteed by happens-before in the second way.

Update:

A pseudo-implementation of EBR for multiple readers and a single writer is as follows:

#include <atomic>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

struct ThreadState {
    std::atomic<bool> active{false};
    std::atomic<uint64_t> local_epoch{0};
};

class EBRManager {
    std::atomic<uint64_t> global_epoch{0};
    ThreadState thread_states[8]; 
    
    // Bag[0], Bag[1], Bag[2]
    std::vector<void*> garbage_bags[3];

public:

    void reader_enter(int tid) {
        thread_states[tid].active.store(true, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
        uint64_t g = global_epoch.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst);
        thread_states[tid].local_epoch.store(g, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
    }

    void reader_exit(int tid) {
        thread_states[tid].active.store(false, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
    }

    
    void retire(void* old_ptr) {
        uint64_t g = global_epoch.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        garbage_bags[g].push_back(old_ptr);
        try_collect();
    }

    void try_collect() {
        uint64_t curr_g = global_epoch.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst);

        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
            if (thread_states[i].active.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst)) {
                if (thread_states[i].local_epoch.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst) != curr_g) {
                    return; 
                }
            }
        }


        uint64_t next_g = (curr_g + 1) % 3;
        

        uint64_t safe_g = (next_g + 1) % 3; 
        clear_bag(safe_g);

        global_epoch.store(next_g, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
    }

    void clear_bag(int index) {
        for (void* ptr : garbage_bags[index]) {
            free(ptr); 
        }
        garbage_bags[index].clear();
    }
};

struct Data {
    int value;
};

std::atomic<Data*> global_ptr{new Data{100}};
EBRManager ebr;

void writer_thread_update(int new_value) {
   Data* newData = new Data{new_value};
   Data* oldData = global_ptr.exchange(newData, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
   if (oldData != nullptr) {
      ebr.retire(oldData); 
   }
}

void reader_thread(int tid) {
   ebr.reader_enter(tid);
   Data* p = global_ptr.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst);
   ebr.reader_exit(tid);
}

My approach to proof:

As shown in the graph, we don't need to care about what the value of epoch at #1 reads; we can just assume that the value is C. Assuming the operation value.fetch_add(0,std::memory_order::acq_rel) at #2 reads the pointer value Px, we also don't need to care about what the writer does before, because the pointer value Px can only potentially be reclaimed after it is swapped out. So, we assume there exists a writer that executes an exchange operation that writes new_pointer and swaps out Px, because of the release sequence, this means, for any reader who reads the pointer value Px at #2 must synchronize with such a operation at #3 that swapped out Px and write new_pointer; therefore, its #1 must be visible to #4 of the writer. This is the core idea why I think fetch_add(0,acq_rel) can hold the same correctness as the first example does.

As shown in the picture, the epoch can at most be advanced once if the stored epoch of all readers reading Px equal G and the writer subsequently reclaims the pointer value saved in garbage[G-1]; anyway, Px was saved in garbage[G], the epoch cannot be advanced until all readers reading Px write false to active. This proof applies to any reader.
rows.key_body:
NOT Equal guaranteed

Regarding your question:

Does the observable behavior of the program guaranteed by seq_cst equal that of changing it to RMW operations with acq_rel that write the same value?

No, not in general. A no-op RMW with `acq_rel` is not a drop-in replacement for a `seq_cst` load/store pair.

Only equivilant correctness (in special cases)

For the small example in the question, though,

If we only consider the correctness of implementing the core idea, can I change the memory order seq_cst to acq_rel by changing the corresponding operations to those in the second example? IIUC, they should have the same correctness; merely, the visibility of #1 is guaranteed by the single total order in the first way, and is guaranteed by happens-before in the second way

..the particular implication you want does hold.

See [atomics.order] in the C++23.

Different from other answers, I could find no results anywhere for this specific error:

git pull --prune

error: could not delete references: cannot lock ref 'refs/remotes/origin/branchname': Unable to create 'C:/develop/repo/.git/refs/remotes/origin/branchname.lock': File exists.
 
Another git process seems to be running in this repository, e.g.
an editor opened by 'git commit'. Please make sure all processes
are terminated then try again. If it still fails, a git process
may have crashed in this repository earlier:
remove the file manually to continue. From github.com/repo

annoyingly, it is trying to cleanup 100s of branches that were deleted on the server... each time I run a pull or fetch, it does the same mass deletion, making no progress :(
rows.key_body:
Looking in the folder, C:/develop/repo/.git/refs/remotes/origin/ there are no lock files.

There are no other git processes or anti-virus programs running (a typical culprit).

What I ended up doing was search (insensitive, -i) for the branch:

git pull --prune | grep -i branchname

 - [deleted]                 (none)     -> origin/BRANCHNAME
 - [deleted]                 (none)     -> origin/branchname

What I discovered, there was two branches on the server with the same name attempting to be deleted. NEITHER was on my machine. "List Remote" command helps here.

git ls-remote | grep -i xyz

What this means for Windows systems which have CaSe in-Sensitive file-systems, you cannot have two files with the same name in the directory. Git is trying to create both ".lock' files, but only 1 can exist, so it fails with "File exists" error message.

The error message is misleading... the solution (aside from re-cloning) is to delete all references to the branch refs from your hidden .git folder. Those refs are stored in 3 files in my case:

.git/info/refs

.git/packed-refs

.git/FETCH_HEAD

I used the SED command to remove the lines in-place

sed -i '\|dev-1234$|Id' .git/info/refs .git/packed-refs .git/FETCH_HEAD

--- similar error message which gets more search hits, if you have a local branch (dev-1) with one case, and upstream changes to the other (DEV-1) case ---

error: cannot lock ref 'refs/remotes/origin/DEV-1': 'refs/remotes/origin/DEV-1' exists; cannot create 'refs/remotes/origin/DEV-1'

! [new branch] DEV-1 -> origin/DEV-1 (unable to update local ref)

rows.body:
Consider an array of a permutation P of length n (n > 2), namely some order of the integers 1 through n.

Example of P with length n = 7, [6,5,2,3,7,1,4]

A "score" of a permutation is measured by the amount of indices i (0 <= i <= n-3) that satisfy the condition, P[i] >= P[i+1] + P[i+2].

The score of the example P is 2 at i = 1, 5 (5 >= 2 + 3, 7 >= 1 + 4)

Could we find the maximum score among all possible permutation of length n?

Here are some bruteforce solutions:

n = 3; max = 1 (3 2 1)
n = 4; max = 2 (4 3 1 2)
n = 5; max = 2 (5 4 3 1 2)
n = 6; max = 2 (6 4 2 1 3 5)
n = 7; max = 3 (7 5 1 4 6 3 2)*
n = 8; max = 4 (8 5 3 2 7 6 1 4)
n = 9; max = 4 (9 8 5 3 2 7 6 1 4)
n = 10; max = 5 (10 8 2 6 9 5 4 1 3 7)
n = 11; max = 5 (11 10 8 2 6 9 5 4 1 3 7)
n = 12; max = 6 (12 7 3 4 10 9 1 6 11 8 2 5)
.
n = 15; max (currently) = 8; (15 13 1 11 9 2 7 14 10 4 6 12 8 3 5)
.
n = 20; max (currently) = 10 (20 15 1 10 19 14 2 9 18 13 3 8 17 12 4 7 16 11 5 6)

There seems to be a strategy of placeing digits in this manner:

20 15 1 10
19 14 2 9
18 13 3 8
17 12 4 7 
16 11 5 6

to achieve a 5 blocks of score = 2. But the solution of n = 15 with max = 8 suggests otherwise by joining 2 score 2 blocks

15 13 1 11
        11 9 2 7 | 14 10 4 6 | 12 8 3 5

Could we possibly find a formula or an optimal strategy for this? Thank you!
rows.key_body:
I adopted a Divide And Conquer strategy which can be described as follows.

Suppose we want to find an optimally scoring permutation of A = {1, ... , n}. Choose usize and vsize so that usize + 2 + vsize = n. Let U be any subset of A of size usize.

Suppose p,q, p != q, are in A and not in U, define S(U,p,q) as the optimal score attainable from permutations of elements of U followed by p then q. Define V = A - U - {p,q} and T(p,q,V) as the optimal score attainable from p, q then permutations of elements of V. Then the maximum score attainable by any permutation of elements of A is

MAX_{U,p,q} S(U,p,q) + T(p,q,V)

My naive O(n!) permutation 'brute force' exhaustive search program gave me (3 7 12 11 1 10 8 2 6 13 9 4 5) and (5 12 11 1 9 13 10 3 7 14 8 6 2 4) for n=13 and 14 scoring 6 and 7 respectively.

My not-production-level-tested exhaustive O(n^2(nCk)k!) for k = floor((n-1)/2) permutation divide and conquer program found examples of optimal sequences for n = 15, to 22 inclusive, (13 11 2 8 7 1 5 14 10 4 6 15 12 3 9), (12 10 2 8 6 1 5 14 15 11 4 7 16 13 3 9), (13 9 4 5 15 8 7 1 6 16 12 2 10 17 14 3 11), (12 10 2 6 13 9 4 5 17 14 3 11 18 16 1 15 7 8), (16 11 5 6 15 12 3 9 8 1 7 18 14 4 10 19 17 2 13), (18 13 5 8 16 9 7 1 6 19 15 4 11 20 17 3 14 12 2 10) , (13 16 12 4 8 17 10 7 2 5 20 19 1 18 14 3 11 21 15 6 9), (17 12 5 7 19 16 3 13 11 1 8 21 15 6 9 22 20 2 18 14 4 10) with scores 8, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 11 and 12 respectively.
rows.title: Finding a maximum "score" of a permutation

rows.body:
I want to use circular queue with different types and lengths in a project which mainly consists of C code. I'm thinking about implementing the circular queue as a C++ template struct. How to expose the fully specialized C++ template struct to C?

// C++ implementation
// queue.hpp
template <typename T, size_t MAX_LEN>
struct Queue {
    T data[MAX_LEN];
    size_t readIdx = 0;
    size_t writeIdx = 0;

    bool PushBack(T);
    bool PopFront(T *);
};

// expected C API
typedef struct {
    int data[8];
    size_t readIdx;
    size_t writeIdx;
} Qint8;
bool Qint8_PushBack(Qint8 *, int);
bool Qint8_PopFront(Qint8 *, int *);
// C code won't access struct members directly
// but should be able to know the struct's size
// e.g. define an instance, or embed the circular queue in anouther struct
extern Qint8 g_qint8;

typedef struct {
    char data[4];
    size_t readIdx;
    size_t writeIdx;
} Qchar4;
bool Qchar4_PushBack(Qchar4 *, char);
bool Qchar4_PopFront(Qchar4 *, char *);
rows.key_body:
I've got an idea: expose the concrete type Qint8 and Qchar4 as memory buffers.

// bridge.h
#pragma once
#include <stdalign.h>
#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif

#define Qint8Size 48
#define Qint8Align 8
typedef struct {
    alignas(Qint8Align) unsigned char internal[Qint8Size];
} Qint8;
void Qint8_Construct(Qint8 *);
bool Qint8_PushBack(Qint8 *, int);
bool Qint8_PopFront(Qint8 *, int *);
// C code won't access struct members directly
// but should be able to know the struct's size
// e.g. define an instance, or embed the circular queue in anouther struct
extern Qint8 g_qint8;

#define Qchar4Size 24
#define Qchar4Align 8
typedef struct {
    alignas(Qchar4Align) unsigned char internal[Qchar4Size];
} Qchar4;
void Qchar4_Construct(Qchar4 *);
bool Qchar4_PushBack(Qchar4 *, char);
bool Qchar4_PopFront(Qchar4 *, char *);

#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif

// bridge.cpp
#include "bridge.h"
#include "queue.hpp"
#include <new>
using T1 = Queue<int, 8>;
static_assert(sizeof(T1) == Qint8Size && sizeof(Qint8) == Qint8Size);
static_assert(alignof(T1) == Qint8Align);

void Qint8_Construct(Qint8 *q) { new(q->internal) T1; }
bool Qint8_PushBack(Qint8 *q, int v) {
    auto p = std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T1 *>(q->internal));
    return p->PushBack(v);
}
bool Qint8_PopFront(Qint8 *q, int *v) {
    auto p = std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T1 *>(q->internal));
    return p->PopFront(v);
}

using T2 = Queue<char, 4>;
static_assert(sizeof(T2) == Qchar4Size && sizeof(Qchar4) == Qchar4Size);
static_assert(alignof(T2) == Qchar4Align);
void Qchar4_Construct(Qchar4 *q) { new(q->internal) T2; }
bool Qchar4_PushBack(Qchar4 *q, char v) {
    auto p = std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T2 *>(q->internal));
    return p->PushBack(v);
}
bool Qchar4_PopFront(Qchar4 *q, char *v) {
    auto p = std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T2 *>(q->internal));
    return p->PopFront(v);
}

This works. The downside is the hardcode of queue size and alignment in the header.
rows.title: Is it possible to expose C++ template struct (fully specialized) to C?

I'm trying to launch my OpenGL application using RenderDoc, but I keep getting the following error:

[error] A debug OpenGL context was requested but not provided by the driver

The application runs perfectly fine when launched directly from Visual Studio. However, when I try to launch the same executable through RenderDoc, it fails.

I'm using GLFW, and the debug context is requested using the following line:

glfwWindowHint(GLFW_OPENGL_DEBUG_CONTEXT, result->debugContextRequested_ ? GLFW_TRUE : GLFW_FALSE);

I've also run OpenGLGP.exe --diagnostics, and the results indicate that my system supports the required OpenGL features:

Vendor: Intel
Renderer: Intel(R) Graphics
OpenGL: 4.5.0 - Build 32.0.101.8860
GLSL: 4.50 - Build 32.0.101.8860
Core profile: yes
Debug context: yes
Compliant: yes

I'm using RenderDoc 1.46.

What confuses me is that the diagnostics confirm debug context support, yet RenderDoc reports that the driver does not provide it.

My questions are:

  • What exactly does "not provided by the driver" mean in this context?

  • Why would the application work in Visual Studio but fail when launched through RenderDoc?

  • What settings or potential compatibility issues should I check?

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!
rows.key_body:
“Not provided by the driver” probably comes from your application’s check after creation. It means the resulting context lacks the expected debug flag; it does not establish that the driver misses debug-context support. Search your code for that exact message to confirm its origin.

After making the window’s context current and initializing your OpenGL loader, you can inspect the result:

GLint flags = 0;
glGetIntegerv(GL_CONTEXT_FLAGS, &flags);

bool debugContext = (flags & GL_CONTEXT_FLAG_DEBUG_BIT) != 0;

If you use RenderDoc’s in-application API, enable validation before creating the GLFW window:

rdoc_api->SetCaptureOptionU32(
    eRENDERDOC_Option_APIValidation, 1);

The option controls enabling graphics API debugging features. RenderDoc API documentation

If enabling it does not resolve the failure, compare the executable, command-line arguments, working directory, and context flags between both launches. Also check whether your application changes RenderDoc capture options before creating the context. The supplied evidence points first to RenderDoc’s debug-bit override; it does not establish an Intel driver compatibility bug.
rows.title: "A debug OpenGL context was requested but not provided by the driver" when launching an application that works in Visual Studio

rows.body:
Consider this simple code.

struct Foo {
    template <typename T>
    struct Bar {
        ~Bar();
    };
};

with the out-of-line implementation

template <typename T>
Foo::Bar<T>::~Bar()
{
    // dtor implementation
}

Using clang (up to current trunk), with -std=c++20 and -Wdtor-name issues a warning: warning: ISO C++ requires the name after '::~' to be found in the same scope as the name before '::~' [-Wdtor-name], and requires the implementation be changed to this.

template <typename T>
Foo::Bar<T>::~Bar<T>()
{
    // dtor implementation
}

But, CWG 2237 makes this invalid (at least in a plain class template). Maybe it wasn't intended to extend to a nested class template, or maybe clang has a bug?

FWIW, gcc (current trunk) accepts the first one, and issues a compile warning for the second: warning: template-id not allowed for destructor in C++20 [-Wtemplate-id-cdtor]

Note that when using -Werror (which I do), these warnings are errors.

I assume this is a clang bug, but before I filed one, I wanted to make sure my understanding wasn't way off base.
rows.key_body:
This is the warning for CWG244. It is saying that in "nested-name-specifier class-name :: ~ class-name", the second class-name is looked up in the same scope as the first nested-name-specifier, and not in the scope of the first class-name. Clang is claiming to use an extension to search inside the first class-name to find the destructor (because searching inside Foo:: will not be able to find a ~Bar).

The warning is suggesting you write it like:

template <typename T>
Foo::Bar<T>::Bar::~Bar()
{
    // dtor implementation
}

Where now the first nested-name-specifier is Foo::Bar<T>::, which you will be able to find ~Bar in.

I'm not sure this warning is actually correct. The part about destructor lookup (now at [basic.lookup.qual.general]p4 was changed heavily by P1787R6, which the discussion around CWG244 and related issues seems to say solves this
rows.title: Is clang broken with `-std=c++20` and `-Wdtor-name`

rows.body:
I would like to make a class that satisfies std::copy_constructible concept and in addition can be constructed from an arbitrary copy constructible value much like std::any does:

#include <concepts>

struct B {
    B(std::copy_constructible auto);
};
static_assert(std::copy_constructible<B>);

But unlike std::any the constructor template B(std::copy_constructible auto) receives its argument by value and not by reference. I expected that based on class.copy.ctor#5, such constructor is never instantiated for B type itself.

B must have implicitly defined copy and move constructors, which must satisfy the concept checking in the assertion. And indeed, GCC accepts the program just fine.

But MSVC dislikes it, gives a weird message about some uninitialized symbol:

<source>(8): error C2131: expression did not evaluate to a constant
<source>(8): note: failure was caused by a read of an uninitialized symbol

As well as Clang, which is more clear in its complains:

error: satisfaction of constraint 'constructible_from<_Tp, _Tp &>' depends on itself
note: while checking the satisfaction of concept 'copy_constructible<B>' requested here

Fortunately, both MSVC and Clang can be made happy by defining 4 user constructors:

struct B {
    B(const B&);
    B(B&&);
    B(B&);
    B(const B&&);
    B(std::copy_constructible auto);
};
static_assert(std::copy_constructible<B>);

Online demo: https://gcc.godbolt.org/z/rTh33cMG3

Which implementation is correct here?

P.S. There is a related question Class with constructor template requiring copyable argument is not copyable by itself, but it is about a simpler predicate std::is_copy_constructible_v and Clang's bug, which is fixed already in trunk.
rows.key_body:
To decide which constructors are right, go back to the basic:

There are 3 types of constructors, and 2 associated assignment operators:

B::B();           // the default constructor.
B::B(const B&);   // the copy constructor.
B::B(B&&);        // the move constructor.

B& B::operator=(const B&);  // copy assignment
B& B::operator=(B&&);       // move assignment

You should memorize these declarations, they are that important, and you will need them quite often enough.

Since your class has custom contruction needs, is copyable and moveable, you should apply the rule of 5. In effect, you should first define all 5 of these functions, with the same exact parameter definitions, even if using = default will work just fine.

Then define your custom template constructor, and, if your constructor is not declared explicit, its associated assignment operator.

B::B(std::copy_constructible auto&& x) { *this =  x; }  // consider whether you want to declare this constructor 'explicit'

template <std::copy_constructible T>
B& B::operator=(T&& x) { 
   // do whatever it takes to store x, use std::forward<T>(x) as necessary 
   // to let the compiler move data from x if possible
   return *this;
}

For template constructors, use perfect forwarding (&&), so the caller can chose whether to make a copy of the parameter or attempt to move it using std::move().

As a general rule, avoid constructors and assingment operators accepting non-const references (as in B::B(B&)), as a constructor, or assignment that changes the parameter would be quite confusing, and const move references (as in B::B(const B&&)), since one cannot move, but only copy a const object.
rows.title: What constructors must be defined to satisfy copy constructible concept for any-like class?

rows.body:
At work, I am running 3.9.21. At home, I am running Python 3.13.2 on Linux, but also use uv install Python 3.9.21 to be in sync with work.

In my home machine, I created a new project:

uv init --package --python "python==3.9.21" sandbox
cd sandbox
uv sync

At this time, I got the following error:

Using CPython 3.13.2
error: The requested interpreter resolved to Python 3.13.2, which is incompatible with the project's Python requirement: `==3.9.21`

How can I create a project with this specific version (3.9.21) of Python?
rows.key_body:
I tried your steps in my macbook and they worked fine without any error.

Your error sounds as if uv was installed via pip install uv under Python 3.13.2. Could that be?

This is why Astral (who programmed uv) warns not to install uv simply with pip install uv. Because then, the uv gets dependent on the particular Python version. But the point of uv is that it should be in the level on top of the Python versions and manage them.

Your uv seems to be installed under Python 3.13.2, thus fixed to it - which is suboptimal. And it has performance penalties - you are not using uv (Rust's) actual speed - but uv inside pip.

The solution in this case would be:

  1. uninstall pip uninstall uv
  2. globally install uv
# macos and linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# windows
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

or just look in https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/#__tabbed_1_2

And with the global uv your steps should work without problems.

--

Pip install might make only if e.g. you are in a Docker container where you know, there will be only one Python version forever. But even then, I wouldn't use pip install uv actually.

Probably your solution

I see the problem is, that you have to pin your Python version. @IRFANAASLAM was close to the solution.

First, however, you should check in your parent folder of your project, whether you accidentally ran there uv init in the past. Is there a pyproject.toml or .python-version file? Or a .venv folder? If so, delete them all! Because they can interfere with anything you do in your project folder - I've recently read.

Second, in your work project folder - or your home project folder - the best is in both - ensure that you do:

uv python install 3.9.21
uv python pin 3.9.21

uv python pin 3.9.21 would create a .python-version file in your computer. Transferring the .python-version file together with pyproject.toml and uv.lock would be sufficient to ensure the correct Python version for your project.

A question would be: Is your home computer a Windows? And couldn't it be that there is a problem with Python versions at home? (Does a 3.9.21 Python exist for your OS? - If not, it could use 3.13.2 out of lack of the correct version - as the next fallback). If so, I would highly recommend you, to use WSL2 (windows subsystem for Linux), where you can install ubuntu or any other linux into your WSL virtual machine and run linux in windows - while having all the files in your windows available.

Ah I see you aid at home you installed using curl. That means - you have a macos? Probably with ARM architecture? - But I see it can't be the problem, because I have ARM and 3.9.21 exists there.

You could e.g. in your work computer do:

uv python pin 3.9.21
uv lock

This updates the .python-version and uv.lock file.

At home then, transfer your pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .python-version file to your home project folder. No pyproject.toml file should be present in the parent folder(s) to be sure.

If you run now

uv sync

It should sync correctly and recreate the project's environment.

You have to use the pyproject.toml from your work. And the uv.lock and .python-version file.

the .python-version file just contains the version number. Its content in this case is simply "3.9.21". So one could also just generate it manually.
rows.title: Create project with specific (downgraded) Python version

When opening and closing my Menu and the drop down animation of the Menu is kind of glitchy now. This didn't happen before in iOS 18, so wondering if my code is inherently wrong or if this is a bug.

Here is an MRE of what I am doing in my actual app. Could someone please see If they are getting the same? I am getting the message in iOS 26.1 and 26.2.

        NavigationStack {
            ZStack {

rows.key_body:
In my case, I was getting the same warning and animation glitch when a Menu was inside a GlassEffectContainer with .buttonStyle(.glass) and .glassEffectUnion().

Adding .compositingGroup() before the button style fixed it:

Menu {
    // menu content...
} label: {
    Image(systemName: "ellipsis")
}
.compositingGroup()     //  fixes _UIReparentingView warning
.buttonStyle(.glass)

The .compositingGroup() creates a rendering boundary that isolates the Menu from parent effects, preventing the UIKit view hierarchy conflict when the menu presents.

Even if you're not using glass effects, .compositingGroup() on its own might still resolve your issue since it seems to be a general SwiftUI/Menu bug in iOS 26 related to how Menu's UIKit presentation interacts with the view hierarchy.
rows.title: iOS 26 broken view hierarchy on Menu

/**
 * Vector addition: C = A + B.
 *
 * This sample is a very basic sample that implements element by element
 * vector addition. It is the same as the sample illustrating Chapter 2
 * of the programming guide with some additions like error checking.
 */

#include <stdio.h>

// For the CUDA runtime routines (prefixed with "cuda_")
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#include <helper_cuda.h>
/**
 * CUDA Kernel Device code
 *
 * Computes the vector addition of A and B into C. The 3 vectors have the same
 * number of elements numElements.
 */
__global__ void vectorAdd(const float *A, const float *B, float *C, int numElements)
{
    int i = blockDim.x * blockIdx.x + threadIdx.x;

    if (i < numElements) {
        C[i] = A[i] + B[i] + 0.0f;
    }
}

/**
 * Host main routine
 */
int main(void)
{
    // Error code to check return values for CUDA calls
    cudaError_t err = cudaSuccess;

    // Print the vector length to be used, and compute its size
    int    numElements = 50000;
    size_t size        = numElements * sizeof(float);
    printf("[Vector addition of %d elements]\n", numElements);

    // Allocate the host input vector A
    float *h_A = (float *)malloc(size);

    // Allocate the host input vector B
    float *h_B = (float *)malloc(size);

    // Allocate the host output vector C
    float *h_C = (float *)malloc(size);

    // Verify that allocations succeeded
    if (h_A == NULL || h_B == NULL || h_C == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate host vectors!\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Initialize the host input vectors
    for (int i = 0; i < numElements; ++i) {
        h_A[i] = rand() / (float)RAND_MAX;
        h_B[i] = rand() / (float)RAND_MAX;
    }

    // Allocate the device input vector A
    float *d_A = NULL;
    err        = cudaMalloc((void **)&d_A, size);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate device vector A (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Allocate the device input vector B
    float *d_B = NULL;
    err        = cudaMalloc((void **)&d_B, size);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate device vector B (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Allocate the device output vector C
    float *d_C = NULL;
    err        = cudaMalloc((void **)&d_C, size);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to allocate device vector C (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Copy the host input vectors A and B in host memory to the device input
    // vectors in
    // device memory
    printf("Copy input data from the host memory to the CUDA device\n");
    err = cudaMemcpy(d_A, h_A, size, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to copy vector A from host to device (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    err = cudaMemcpy(d_B, h_B, size, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to copy vector B from host to device (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Launch the Vector Add CUDA Kernel
    int threadsPerBlock = 256;
    int blocksPerGrid   = (numElements + threadsPerBlock - 1) / threadsPerBlock;
    printf("CUDA kernel launch with %d blocks of %d threads\n", blocksPerGrid, threadsPerBlock);
    vectorAdd<<<blocksPerGrid, threadsPerBlock>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, numElements);
    err = cudaGetLastError();

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to launch vectorAdd kernel (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Copy the device result vector in device memory to the host result vector
    // in host memory.
    printf("Copy output data from the CUDA device to the host memory\n");
    err = cudaMemcpy(h_C, d_C, size, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to copy vector C from device to host (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Verify that the result vector is correct
    for (int i = 0; i < numElements; ++i) {
        if (fabs(h_A[i] + h_B[i] - h_C[i]) > 1e-5) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Result verification failed at element %d!\n", i);
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }
    }

    printf("Test PASSED\n");

    // Free device global memory
    err = cudaFree(d_A);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to free device vector A (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    err = cudaFree(d_B);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to free device vector B (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    err = cudaFree(d_C);

    if (err != cudaSuccess) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to free device vector C (error code %s)!\n", cudaGetErrorString(err));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Free host memory
    free(h_A);
    free(h_B);
    free(h_C);

    printf("Done\n");
    return 0;
}

the expected JIT output for Program:Main() should be:

mov edi, 10

tail.jmp [Program:Consume(Program+Point)]

I would sidestep the whole issue by creating simple get_lo () and get_hi () accessor functions to extract the relevant halves of your int64 and call them when needed:

#include <cstdint>

std::uint32_t get_lo (std::uint64_t combined) { return static_cast <std::uint32_t> (combined); }

rows.body:
A debug print line seems to make code execution unexpectedly faster. Commenting out a printf that is conditional on n<100 slows things down when n is much larger.

How is the conditional print that never executes for n>100 speeding things up?

This toy code arises from a question on Math SE What is the most efficient way to determine if a natural number N can be written as the sum of two squares?. It is a surprisingly tough problem with a single thread unvectorised solution taking around 4 hours to count them out to 109.

That question gives a naïve algorithm which is easy to check and asks if there is a faster way. I thought that avoiding multiplies and sqrt in the main loop would speed it up even if it remains O(sqrt(N)).

This is my first attempt. The odd thing was that my initial routine with a debug print in for small n was actually faster than any of my later attempts to simplify and optimise it once I had it working.

The least subtle behaviour applying to both MSVC and Intel ICX compilers is that commenting out a debugging conditional printf slows things down! In the case of Intel ICX 2025.2.1 by almost 30% (MSVC by 2.5%).

I'm at a loss to explain this. Intel generated code is also notably faster than MSVC. I may be missing something obvious. Timings table - power of 10 increase in N roughly increases computation time by 32x.

N count MSVC time/s MSVC debug time/s ICX time/s ICX debug time/s
10 7 0 0 0 0.001
100 43 0.001 0.001 0 0.002
1000 330 0.001 0.001 0 0.002
10000 2749 0.002 0.002 0 0.003
100000 24028 0.019 0.024 0.013 0.013
1000000 216341 0.474 0.473 0.409 0.297
10000000 1985459 13.402 12.915 11.726 7.835
100000000 18457846 410.982 398.544 368.854 245.783

I had expected that deleting the debugging test code which prints a solution for N<100 would speed things up. But the opposite was the case. I have repeated the timings several times because I didn't believe what I was seeing.

I also found that the fairly simple code for sum_2squares shown below is very hard to optimise further (but that is a story for another question). This is the test code - most interesting speed difference is on the Intel ICX 2025.2.1 compiler:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>
#include <time.h>

bool sum_2squares(unsigned int n)
{
    unsigned int a2, b2, delta_a, delta_b, sum, limit = (unsigned int) sqrt(n);
    a2 = 0;
    delta_a = 1;
    b2 = limit * limit;
    delta_b = 2 * limit - 1;
    while (a2 <= n / 2)
    {
        sum = a2 + b2;
        if (sum == n) // solution
        {
//            if (n<100) printf("%u = %3u + %3u = %3u^2 + %u^2\n", n, a2, b2, (delta_a-1)/2, (delta_b+1)/2);  // commenting this debugging line slows it down!
            return true;
        }
        a2 += delta_a;
        delta_a += 2;
        if (sum > n)
        {
            delta_a -= 2;
            a2 -= delta_a;
            b2 -= delta_b;
            delta_b = delta_b - 2;
        }
    }
    return n == sum;
}

int main()
{
    unsigned int count = 0;
    unsigned int limit = 10;
    time_t start, end;
    start = clock();
    printf("N\t count\t time/s\n");
    for (unsigned int i = 1; i <= 10000000; i++) // runtime about 20s (gets 30x slower
    {
        if (sum_2squares(i)) count++;
        if (i % limit == 0)
        {
            printf("%-9u %-9u  ", i, count);
            end = clock();
            printf("%6.3f\n", (float)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);

            limit *= 10;
        }
    }
}

The timing behaviour is reproducible on Godbolt test range reduced for runtime <2s. Timings can be a bit erratic there. The speed difference is only about 10% on the latest 2026.0 version but still present.

I'm guessing the test and branch which is never taken somehow prevents a pipeline stall. But it is just a guess. I couldn't really spot an obvious cause. I'd like to understand better what is going on. Any other speed enhancements are welcome too.

UPDATE: Guided by the disassembly and profiling I created a straightjacket to force the compiler to generate code that allocates 64bit and 32 bit variables in the same fashion as the faster conditional printf code.

This has worked in the sense that the resulting code is now faster 7s vs 11s and uncommenting the conditional printf line now adds 0.5s to the execution time. This is a useful result but is by no means a satisfactory answer. The compiler by default is generating substandard code for this admittedly strange branch dense code. The flaw appears to be in the compilers register allocation algorithm and/or branch target destination(s) when the simpler code is presented to it.

This also allowed a tidy of the logic with advantage (previously the code was crippled if the addition to a2 was not in the outer loop. Original lines commented out below to show the changes made.

This is the latest go-faster version of sum_squares (needs #include <stdint.h>).

bool sum_2squares(uint64_t n) //fastest found so far
{
    uint64_t a2, b2,  limit = sqrt(n);;
    uint64_t delta_a;
    uint32_t delta_b, sum;
    a2 = 0;
    delta_a = 1;
    b2 = limit * limit;
    delta_b = 2 * limit - 1;
    while (a2 <= n / 2)
    {
        sum = a2 + b2;
        if (sum == n) // solution
        {
 //           if (n<2) printf("%I64u = %I64u + %I64u = %I64u^2 + %u^2\n", n, a2, b2, (delta_a-1)/2, (delta_b+1)/2);  // slows down if not commented out (as expected)
            return true;
        }
//        a2 += delta_a;
        if (sum > n)
        {
//            a2 -= delta_a;
            b2 -= delta_b;
            delta_b = delta_b - 2;
        }
        else
        { 
            a2 += delta_a;
            delta_a += 2;
        }      
    }
    return n == sum;
}

It includes the tweak of making delta_a 64 bit which was discovered by tweaking the code one variable at a time to the other size.

The code can be crippled by making either of the main outer variables base or i (for loop counter) 64 bit. The code can be slowed down ~1s by making limit 32 bit. The code is almost agnostic about the width of sum, delta_A and delta_b.

Having obtained what I though was the best possible code I then flipped each integer variable type in turn from 32 to 64 bit or vice versa to measure the timing effect. Results are ranked by influence.

variable 32 64 flip time/s
main base # 12.95
main i # 12.05
limit # 8.34
a2 # 7.47
main count # 7.15
b2 # 7.15
sum # 7.06
delta_b # 7.0
delta_a # 6.9
original - - 7.08

# indicates the type of the integer variable in the enhanced original code.

The big surprise was that promoting delta_a to 64 bits speeds thing up slightly (not by much but enough to be measurable and reproducible). Behaviour may vary with platform and compiler - be interested to know if this version also runs faster on the M4/AMD/ARM CPUs.

I'm aware there are lots of sum of two squares questions on SO already and that the Hermite-Serret algorithm might be the method of choice here but in this question I am concerned with the weird effect of a conditional print on the speed of a brute force attack.

Instead of polluting the issue with extra calls to printf in the inner loop, let's just add some instrumentation to compute statistics. Here is a version that counts the number of tests:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>
#include <time.h>

unsigned long stats[4];
#define STAT(i)  stats[i]++

#ifndef STAT
#define STAT(i)
#endif

bool sum_2squares(unsigned int n)
{
    unsigned int limit = (unsigned int)+sqrt(n);
    unsigned int a2, b2, delta_a, delta_b, sum = 0;
    a2 = 0;
    delta_a = 1;
    b2 = limit * limit;
    delta_b = 2 * limit - 1;
    sum = 0;
    while (a2 <= n / 2) {
        STAT(0);
        sum = a2 + b2;
        if (sum == n) { // solution
            STAT(1);
            return true;
        }
        a2 += delta_a;
        delta_a += 2;
        if (sum > n) {
            STAT(2);
            delta_a -= 2;
            a2 -= delta_a;
            b2 -= delta_b;
            delta_b = delta_b - 2;
        }
    }
    STAT(3);
    return sum == n;
}

int main()
{
    unsigned int count = 0;
    unsigned int limit = 10;
    time_t start, end;
    start = clock();
    for (unsigned int i = 1; i <= 10000000; i++) { // runtime about 20s (gets 30x slower
        if (sum_2squares(i)) count++;
        if (i % limit) continue;
        if (limit == 10) {
            printf("N         count      time/s");
            if (stats[0]) {
                printf("  total loops        alternations       matches        non-matches");
            }
            printf("\n");
        }
        printf("%-9u %-9u  ", i, count);
        end = clock();
        printf("%6.3f", (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);
        if (stats[0]) {
            printf(" %12lu", stats[0]);
            printf(" %12lu %5.2f%%", stats[2], stats[2] * 100.0 / stats[0]);
            printf(" %8lu %6.3f%%",  stats[1], stats[1] * 100.0 / stats[0]);
            printf(" %8lu %6.3f%%",  stats[3], stats[3] * 100.0 / stats[0]);
        }
        printf("\n");
        limit *= 10;
    }
}

100       43          0.000          538           96 17.84%       43  7.993%       57 10.595%
1000      330         0.000        17222         4271 24.80%      330  1.916%      670  3.890%
10000     2749        0.001       556366       150935 27.13%     2749  0.494%     7251  1.303%
100000    24028       0.019     17895109      5002964 27.96%    24028  0.134%    75972  0.425%
1000000   216341      0.271    573416191    162170695 28.28%   216341  0.038%   783659  0.137%
10000000  1985459     7.038  18320889055   5209580480 28.44%  1985459  0.011%  8014541  0.044%

More code, yet almost twice as fast!

My guess is we have a pathological case of branch misprediction with too many branches in the same cache line:

  • the first test is almost always false (branch only taken in 0.044% of tests at 107.
  • the second test is almost always false as well (branch taken except in 0.011% of tests at 107.
  • the third test (alternations) is true in 28% of cases, so mispredicted more than half the time.

If the same prediction hardware is used for the third test and the second or first one (which may be duplicated at the end of the loop), the branch prediction is very ineffective. Smaller code resulting in more branch misprediction, hence slower execution times.

Branch prediction hardware is intrinsic to the actual hardware (Apple silicon M4-pro in my case) and the behavior also depends on the code produced by the compiler, not only which instructions are used but also and sometime predominantly its layout.

I am a bit surprised that the compiler would not ensure optimal code layout to avoid this pathological case of prediction interaction, but the timings seem to point to this explanation.

I am not an expert in these questions, @Peter could you confirm my predictions?
rows.title: Conditional debug print speeds up code execution in sum of two squares problem

I’m trying to install the Entity Framework Core CLI tools globally using the .NET CLI command:

dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef

However, the installation fails with the following error message:

Tool 'dotnet-ef' failed to update due to the following:

The settings file in the tool's NuGet package is invalid: Settings file 'DotnetToolSettings.xml' was not found in the package.
Tool 'dotnet-ef' failed to install. Contact the tool author for assistance.

To reproduce, run dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef in a terminal or command prompt.

What I've tried

  • Running dotnet tool uninstall --global dotnet-ef and reinstalling.

Why is this error occurring, and how can I fix it so that dotnet-ef installs successfully?
rows.key_body:
This is due to a mismatch between the version of the .NET SDK (probably v9.0) and the latest version of the dotnet-ef tool (v10.0). This command tells you which versions you have installed:

dotnet --list-sdks

You can solve it by explicitely specifying a version of the tool that matches your installed .NET SDK. For example, when running on .NET SDK v9.0:

install --global dotnet-ef --version 9.0.11

or

dotnet.exe tool install --global dotnet-ef --version 9.0.11

In Safari on iOS 26, when the page is scrolled down and the address bar shrinks at the bottom, the viewport appears to get displaced vertically, which in turn shifts the position of elements with position "fixed" or "sticky."

Code example: https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/reactjs-playground-forked-6zmgr4

Note the relevant div serving as a fixed footer, with inline styles as follows:

style={{
  position: "fixed",
  bottom: 0,
}}

Navigate to the code sandbox URL on iPhone with iOS 26 to reproduce the issue: https://6zmgr4.csb.app/

Scroll down the page. Notice that the fixed footer isn’t aligned to the bottom of the screen any longer. Rather, there is a gap between the bottom of the viewport and the bottom of the fixed footer as shown in the screenshot. (The text is obstructed in the screenshot; it reads "This should be fixed at the bottom of the screen when I scroll down.")

Screenshot of issue

How can I address this? So far I've tried the following:

  • Various combinations of different css attributes on the document and body elements (position , top , overflow , overscroll-behavior)

  • Adding bottom: -100vh; padding-bottom: calc(100vh + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0)) to the footer (this worked fine in other browsers, but not in Safari 26 beta)

  • Setting the following CSS content:

    html {
  overflow: hidden;
}

body {
  overflow: auto;
}
    • This prevented the issue (footer element shifting on scroll), but it had some undesired side effects. The scroll position doesn’t get maintained any longer when navigating back to the page, and programmatic scroll using window.scrollTo stops working. Also, the address bar doesn’t shrink any longer at the bottom of the screen when the user scrolls down.
rows.key_body:
There are multiple issues and bugs as far as I can tell:

  1. Position: fixed top and bottom toolbar start to drift as you scroll.

  2. editing in text boxes (inputs are better, and textareas much worse) causes conflicts, as it turns off fixed positions, and sometimes they are there, although not visible.

  3. side menus often get cut. A fixed position scrollable side navbar typically gets cut off right above the URL line, but the background continues to be translucent all the way down to the bottom of the screen. This really looks awful.

  4. top and bottom backgrounds randomly become solid (instead of translucent) to try and compensate for the position:fixed items.

Overall, I have to say this is the buggiest release of Safari for quite a few years now...

rows.key_body:
CouchbaseNetClient 3.8.1 references System.Linq.Async (v6.0.1, which is around 3 years old). Via dotnet nuget why:

This version exposes the ToListAsync method. .NET 10 has the same method included in the framework.

Since you have transient dependency on the package you can install it's 7th version which seems to have the ambiguity resolved for .NET 10. as stated in the Recommended action section of the linked before doc:

If you're upgrading to .NET 10 and your code includes a direct package reference to System.Linq.Async, remove that package reference or upgrade to version 7.0.0.

Or for transient dependency (as in your case) you can reference it directly and add <ExcludeAssets> metadata with a value of compile or all:

This configuration prevents direct usage in your code while allowing other packages to continue using System.Linq.Async internally:

<PackageReference Include="System.Linq.Async" Version="6.0.1">
  <ExcludeAssets>compile</ExcludeAssets>
</PackageReference>

Use this configuration only if you're certain no dependencies require System.Linq.Async at runtime.

<PackageReference Include="System.Linq.Async" Version="6.0.1">
  <ExcludeAssets>all</ExcludeAssets>
</PackageReference>

Moving from the comment by Panagiotis Kanavos:

I see that the latest CouchbaseClient, 3.9.0-RC3 removes the dependency on System.Linq.Async on .NET 10.

So another option would be to update to it (or wait for the release)
