I am using Oracle APEX 26.1 and have a human task "Equipment Change Review". The Unified Task List and and Task Details Page were generated by APEX. In the the latter one, I included a form to immediately complete the task (assuming its claimed by the user). This part also works without a flaw. However, if the user instead wants to release the task again using the Actions menu (that was generated by APEX!), the task indeed gets released but I get redirected to an error page that says that the task was not found.

I narrowed a few things down: The task details page lives at /task-details?p12_task_id=10280006769377628&clear=12&session=.... After clicking on Release I get to /task-details?p12_equipmentnr=10000084&session=...&cs=.... Crucially, the first GET-variable goes from p12_task_id to p12_equipmentnr. As a result, the task is not found anymore.

The field P12_EQUIPMENTNR is the PK for the form I created on the task detail page but I don't see why APEX would just start thinking that this is the task PK.

The Release Action (again, as configured by APEX itself) has as Behavior

Type: Redirect to URL
Target URL: #action$release?do=submit
Link Attributes: class="taskActionMenu"

I guess the way to read this is that upon clicking Release in the tasks's action menu, the page is treated as submit with :REQUEST being set to RELEASE. The corresponding process hooked to this (via Server-side Condition) performs the Release (as Human Task - Manage / Type: Release / Task ID item: P12_TASK_ID). Note that this part does indeed work---the task is released.

After that I don't know what APEX is doing, ideally it should just reload the task detail page (which it tries) but for some reason it changes in the URL from p12_task_id to p12_equipmentnr and I would like to figure out the APEX internals that I don't understand yet.
rows.title: Oracle APEX Human Task: Release Action redirects to error page

rows.body:
I'm running into some behavior of std::float16_t (and std::bfloat16_t) that I don't understand.

My understanding and expectation is that:

  • the next std::float16_t after 1024 is 1025.
  • 1024+1025=2049 isn't representable as std::float16_t, so it gets rounded-to-even to 2048.
  • therefore, (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) evaluates to std::float16_t(2048).
  • if I then convert that result to float or double, I should get 2048.0f or 2048.0, respectively.

So I expect that:

  • (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) should be 2048.0f.
  • (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) should be 2048.0.

But, they come out 2049.0f and 2049.0 instead.

Why is this?

Similarly, using std::bfloat16_t instead of std::float16_t, I expect that:

  • (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) should be 256.0f.
  • (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) should be 256.0.

But, they come out 257.0f and 257.0 instead.

I observed this using g++ 15.2.0.

The following C++ program demonstrates this issue:

// Use either of the following
// (no earlier since std::float16_t and std::bfloat16_t were introduced in C++23).
/*
  g++ -std=c++26 -O0 -W -Wall -Werror wtf.cpp -o wtf && ./wtf
  g++ -std=c++23 -O0 -W -Wall -Werror wtf.cpp -o wtf && ./wtf
*/
// Note: I also tried clang++ but couldn't get it to understand std::float16_t
// nor std::bfloat16_t.

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdfloat>

int main(int, char**) {

  std::cout << "std::float16_t:\n";
  std::cout << "    std::nextafter(std::float16_t(1024), std::float16_t(1e6)) = "
            <<      std::nextafter(std::float16_t(1024), std::float16_t(1e6))<<"\n";    // 1025 (correct)
  std::cout << "            sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<              sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2 (correct, std::float16_t is 2 bytes)
  std::cout << "                  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<                    (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2048 (correct-- 2049 isn't representable so rounds to even)
  std::cout << "           (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<             (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2049 (SURPRISE-- I expected 2048)
  std::cout << "          (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<            (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2049 (SURPRISE-- I expected 2048)
  std::cout << "\n";

  std::cout << "std::bfloat16_t:\n";
  std::cout << "    std::nextafter(std::bfloat16_t(128), std::bfloat16_t(1e6)) = "
            <<      std::nextafter(std::bfloat16_t(128), std::bfloat16_t(1e6))<<"\n";   // 129 (correct)
  std::cout << "            sizeof(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<              sizeof(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 2 (correct, std::bfloat16_t is 2 bytes)
  std::cout << "                  (std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<                    (std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 256 (correct-- 257 isn't representable so rounds to even)
  std::cout << "           (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<             (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 257 (SURPRISE-- I expected 256)
  std::cout << "          (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<            (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 257 (SURPRISE-- I expected 256)
  std::cout << "\n";

}

Output is:

std::float16_t:
    std::nextafter(std::float16_t(1024), std::float16_t(1e6)) = 1025
            sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2
                  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2048
           (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2049 <-- SURPRISE
          (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2049 <-- SURPRISE

std::bfloat16_t:
    std::nextafter(std::bfloat16_t(128), std::bfloat16_t(1e6)) = 129
            sizeof(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 2
                  (std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 256
           (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 257  <-- SURPRISE
          (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 257  <-- SURPRISE

UPDATE: Here is another head scratcher, not involving any explicit casts at all.

(This variant is actually closer to what happened in real life that led to me posting this question.)

What happens in the following program is that an expectation fails because two things are unexpectedly unequal. That is, the following unexpectedly evaluates to true:

(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) != (std::float16_t(2048))

but then, when the two things are inspected to find out why, they appear to be exactly the same after all.

This is quite mystifying, and makes me question my ability to inspect and debug these issues at all.

What's going on here?

// wtf2.cpp
/*
  g++ -std=c++23 -W -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -Werror wtf2.cpp -o wtf2 && ./wtf2
*/
#include <iostream>
#include <stdfloat>
int main() {
  if ( (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) != (std::float16_t(2048)) ) {
    std::cerr << "Expectation failed: the following are unexpectedly not equal"
              << " (both should be 2048 of size 2):\n";

    std::cerr <<                 "  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))"
              <<            " is "<<(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))
              << " of size "<<sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";
    // output: "(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) is 2048 of size 2"

    std::cerr << "                         (std::float16_t(2048))"
              <<                   " is "<<(std::float16_t(2048))
              <<        " of size "<<sizeof(std::float16_t(2048))<<"\n";
    // output: "(std::float16_t(2048)) is 2048 of size 2"
  }
}

Compile and run (using g++ 15.2.0, target x86_64-linux-gnu):

  g++ -std=c++23 -W -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -Werror wtf2.cpp && ./wtf2

Output is:

Expectation failed: the following are unexpectedly not equal (both should be 2048 of size 2):
  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) is 2048 of size 2
                         (std::float16_t(2048)) is 2048 of size 2
rows.key_body:
It can be either value. An implementation is permitted but not required to represent intermediate expression results with wider precision. ([expr.pre]/6)

The values of the floating-point operands and the results of floating-point expressions may be represented in greater precision and range than that required by the type; the types are not changed thereby.

For GCC, there's the -fexcess-precision= option to control whether to use a wider precision.

I've tried using the standard Tailwind padding and margin utilities like p-4, m-2, space-x-4, and space-y-4 in my HTML. In my first project, these worked perfectly, but in my subsequent projects, they don't seem to apply any styles. I expected that the spacing utilities would be applied correctly, but the elements are not spaced as intended. Instead, I have to manually write the styles in a separate CSS file to get the expected result.
rows.key_body:
I think you are facing this problem just because of your default styling inside your style.css like:

    * {
      box-sizing: border-box;
      margin: 0;
      padding: 0;
    }

In Tailwind v4 you need to use this default styling inside @layer base{}. Put all the default styles inside the Tailwind base layer.

    @layer base {
      * {
        margin: 0;
        padding: 0;
        box-sizing: border-box;
        scroll-behavior: smooth;
      }
    }

I'm trying to set up a low-latency TCP communication channel, but while profiling, I noticed an odd behavior, which I was able to reduce to the following setup:

The simplified structure of the client program is:


write()
wait_for_n_usecs(n)
read()

and for the server it is:

read()
wait_for_n_usecs(n)
write()

However, I noticed that as n increases, the time spent inside read_all() and write_all() also increases (though the rate of increase for write_all is lower than for read_all). Why does doing more work between transfers increase the time spent in these I/O calls?

Some numbers:
When n=5:
    On macOS 11:
         Read time: 32 ms
         Write time: 2 ms
     On Linux 7.2.9:
         Read time: 119 ms
         Write time: 18 ms
When n=50000:
    On macOS 11:
         Read time: 219 ms
         Write time: 12 ms
     On Linux 7.2.9:
        Read time: 153 ms
        Write time: 35 ms

// backend.cpp
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <netinet/tcp.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <csignal>
#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>
#include <chrono>

#define SIZE 20
#define TIMES 256*4

static void die(const char* what){ perror(what); exit(1); }

// Read exactly n bytes (handles partial reads / EINTR)
static void read_all(int fd, uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t got = 0;
    while(got < n){
        ssize_t r = ::read(fd, buf + got, n - got);
        if(r > 0) got += (size_t)r;
        else if(r == 0){ fprintf(stderr, "peer closed connection\n"); exit(1); }
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("read");
    }
}

// Write exactly n bytes (handles partial writes / EINTR)
static void write_all(int fd, const uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t sent = 0;
    while(sent < n){
        ssize_t w = ::write(fd, buf + sent, n - sent);
        if(w >= 0) sent += (size_t)w;
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("write");
    }
}

uint8_t test_buf[SIZE];
uint8_t actual_buf[SIZE];
std::chrono::nanoseconds diff(0);
std::chrono::microseconds read_time(0);
std::chrono::microseconds write_time(0);
std::chrono::nanoseconds time_diff(0);

int main(int argc, char** argv){
    signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);

    int listen_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if(listen_fd < 0) die("socket");

    int one = 1;
    setsockopt(listen_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &one, sizeof(one));

    sockaddr_in addr{};
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_port = htons(9000);
    if(inet_pton(AF_INET, "127.0.0.1", &addr.sin_addr) != 1) die("inet_pton");

    if(bind(listen_fd, (sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr)) < 0) die("bind");
    if(listen(listen_fd, 1) < 0) die("listen");

    int client = accept(listen_fd, nullptr, nullptr);
    if(client < 0) die("accept");

    setsockopt(client, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, sizeof(one));

    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    for(int i=0; i < TIMES; i++){
        auto start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        memset(test_buf, i, SIZE);
        auto end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        diff+=(end1 - start1);

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        read_all(client, actual_buf, SIZE);
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        read_time+=std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(end1-start1);

        #if 1 //Verification of transmission integrity
        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        if (memcmp(test_buf, actual_buf, SIZE)){
            printf("Buffers don't match!\n");
            printf("Offending: %i\n", i);
            exit(1);
        }
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        diff+=(end1 - start1);
        #endif

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        #if 1
        {
            auto s = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
            while((std::chrono::steady_clock::now()-s) < std::chrono::microseconds(50000)){}
        }
        #else
        {
            volatile uint64_t j =0;
            for (uint64_t k=0; k < 5*58315; k++) j++;
        }
        #endif
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        time_diff+=(end1 - start1);

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        write_all(client, actual_buf, SIZE);
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        write_time+=std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(end1-start1);
    }

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    const auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>((end - start)-diff-time_diff);

    uint64_t transfer_size = TIMES*SIZE*2ULL;
    uint64_t transfer_time = duration.count();

    printf("Busy-wait Duration: %lld us\n", (long long)(time_diff.count()/1000));
    printf("Time to complete: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)transfer_time);
    printf("Approximate throughput: %llu GB/s\n", (unsigned long long)((transfer_size/transfer_time)/1000000));

    printf("Read time: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(read_time).count());
    printf("Write time: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(write_time).count());

    close(client);
    close(listen_fd);
}

// client.cpp
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <netinet/tcp.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <csignal>
#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>
#include <chrono>

#define SIZE 20
#define TIMES 256*4

static void die(const char* what){ perror(what); exit(1); }

static void read_all(int fd, uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t got = 0;
    while(got < n){
        ssize_t r = ::read(fd, buf + got, n - got);
        if(r > 0) got += (size_t)r;
        else if(r == 0){ fprintf(stderr, "peer closed connection\n"); exit(1); }
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("read");
    }
}

static void write_all(int fd, const uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t sent = 0;
    while(sent < n){
        ssize_t w = ::write(fd, buf + sent, n - sent);
        if(w >= 0) sent += (size_t)w;
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("write");
    }
}

uint8_t test_buf[SIZE];
uint8_t actual_buf[SIZE];
std::chrono::nanoseconds diff(0);
std::chrono::nanoseconds time_diff(0);

int main(int argc, char** argv){
    signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);

    int client = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if(client < 0) die("socket");

    sockaddr_in addr{};
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_port = htons(9000);
    if(inet_pton(AF_INET, "127.0.0.1", &addr.sin_addr) != 1) die("inet_pton");

    if(connect(client, (sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr)) < 0) die("connect");

    int one = 1;
    setsockopt(client, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, sizeof(one));

    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    for(int i=0; i < TIMES; i++){
        auto start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        memset(test_buf, i, SIZE);
        auto end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        diff+=(end1 - start1);

        write_all(client, test_buf, SIZE);

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        #if 1
        {
            auto s = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
            while((std::chrono::steady_clock::now()-s) < std::chrono::microseconds(50000)){}
        }
        #else
        {
            volatile uint64_t j =0;
            for (uint64_t k=0; k < 5*58315; k++) j++;
        }
        #endif
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        time_diff+=(end1-start1);

        read_all(client, actual_buf, SIZE);

        #if 1 //Verification of transmission integrity
        if (memcmp(test_buf, actual_buf, SIZE)){
            printf("Buffers don't match!\n");
            printf("Offending: %i\n", i);
            exit(1);
        }
        #endif
    }

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    const auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>((end - start) - diff - time_diff);

    uint64_t transfer_size = TIMES*SIZE*2ULL;
    uint64_t transfer_time = duration.count();

    printf("Diff: %lld us\n", (long long)(time_diff.count()/1000));
    printf("Time to complete: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)transfer_time);
    printf("Approximate throughput: %llu GB/s\n", (unsigned long long)((transfer_size/transfer_time)/1000000));

    close(client);
}

Both were compiled with clang++ -std=c++20 -O3

rows.body:
Consider the following code:

char *str = "1234";
long n = strtol(str, &str, 10);

The prototype of strtol() in C99 is:

long strtol(const char *restrict nptr, char **restrict endptr, int base);

My question is: does this call violate the restrict contract and produce undefined behaviour?

I am aware that a similar question has been asked before (Aliased arguments in strtol), but the accepted answer does not clarify my doubts because it lacks of any explanations.

My analysis so far:

As I understand it:

  • const char *restrict nptr promises the compiler that nptr will be the only way to access the memory region defined by the string "1234".

  • char **restrict endptr promises the compiler that endptr will be the only way to access the variable str.

At the point of the call, assuming:

  • the string "1234" is at address 0x100

  • the variable str is at address 0x500

then:

  • nptr = 0x100 (points to the string)

  • endptr = 0x500 (points to the variable str)

The two pointers themselves point to distinct memory locations, so restrict appears to be respected between nptr and endptr directly.

However, note that nptr and *endptr hold the same address. When strtol writes *endptr = ..., it only modifies the variable str, it does not directly access the string "1234". The string would only be accessed through endptr if strtol() performed a double dereference via **endptr.

If an implementation of strtol() were to access the string "1234" via **endptr for any reason, then the restrict promise on nptr would be violated (if one calls strtol(str, &str, 10)), since the string would be accessed through a pointer other than nptr.

The question

Does this constitute a restrict violation according to §6.7.3.1 of C99? Specifically:

  1. Does restrict on endptr only constrain endptr itself, or does it also constrain *endptr with respect to nptr?

  2. If *endptr and nptr point to the same memory, is that sufficient to produce undefined behaviour, even if endptr and nptr themselves are distinct?

  3. Would a hypothetical implementation of strtol() that accesses the string "1234" via **endptr be considered non-conforming to the C99 standard?
rows.key_body:
Since you have tagged this as language-lawyer, then the answer is yes (the call is “legal”) for reasons you may not have expected. However, it is also yes for the reasons you were likely concerned about.

First, as you note, the prototype of strtol is long strtol(const char *restrict nptr, char **restrict endptr, int base);. In this, restrict has no effect. This is because qualifiers are effectively not part of a function type. C 1999 6.7.5.3 15 states that, for purposes of compatibility between function types, “each parameter declared with qualified type is taken as having the unqualified version of its declared type.” This means that long strtol(const char *restrict nptr, char **restrict endptr, int base); has the same effect as long strtol(const char *nptr, char **endptr, int base);; the qualifiers are not part of the function type.

(The qualifiers do affect the code inside a function body, because there the qualifiers are part of the types of the parameters.)

Second, the definition of restrict imposes requirements on code that uses the identifiers (which would be code inside the implementation of the function), not on code that calls a function with qualifiers on its parameters. Therefore, the call is “legal” because it does not violate any requirements related to the qualifiers.

What you are probably wondering about is, if you call strtol as you have shown, would the code inside it satisfy the requirements on the qualifiers. From a language-lawyer perspective, we cannot know this because we cannot know what the code inside the function is. It might not even be C code, but, even if it is, there are ways to implement functions that work with overlapping memory through restricted pointers. Consider this:

void square(double * restrict result, double * restrict x)
{
    double t = *x;
    t = t*t;
    if (result == x)
        *x = t;
    else
        *result = t;
}

This code writes the result to *result without violating the restrict requirements even if x and result point to the same place, because, if they do point to the same place, it uses *x to access that place and does not use *result.

However let’s suppose strtol was written naïvely, oblivious to the possibilities the pointers might point to overlapping memory, so that this strtol reads data through nptr (or expressions based on nptr and not endptr) and writes the end pointer through endptr (or expressions based on endptr and not nptr). Observe that all the objects in memory needed to read the string, those in the array induced by "1234", are completely separate from the str object. The formal definition of restrict in C 1999 6.7.3.1 only imposes requirements on accesses to an object X that is modified during execution of the function (in this situation). They say that if X is accessed with an lvalue based on a restricted pointer, then every access to X will be based on that pointer. For the object str pointed to by endptr, our supposition is this is true: Every access to the object str is through an lvalue based on endptr. For the objects in "1234", there is no modification to those objects, so the formal definition of restrict does not impose any requirements.

Therefore, even a naïve implementation of strtol satisfies the requirements of restrict.
rows.title: Is strtol(str, &str, 10) legal in C99 due to restrict aliasing?

I have two threads communicating through a shared memory-mapped register (flag). Thread 1 runs on a weakly ordered CPU (RISC-V) in an embedded PCIe processor, and Thread 2 runs on the host, which is a x86-64 CPU. The goal is for thread_2() to return only after thread_1() has started (and vice-versa).

Here’s a simplified example:

// Thread 1: RISC-V
void thread_1(volatile int* flag)
{
    *flag = 1;
    while(*flag != 2) {
        membar_read(); // (1)
    }
}

// Thread 2: x86
void thread_2(volatile int* flag)
{
    while(*flag != 1) {}
    *flag = 2;
}

flag is initialized to zero before both threads start. membar_read() is an intrinsic.

Questions

  1. Without the barrier (1), thread 1 spins forever whil thread 2 finishes fine. How is this possible? I thought memory barriers were only to ensure data consistency, not to explicitly "flush" data to other cores. Why does the loop in thread 1 need the barrier to see the value written by thread 2?

  2. Is any additional memory barrier needed for this pattern to be correct? <stdatomic> is available, but I wonder if atomics would be a performance hit compared to using memory barriers or volatile.

rows.body:
I am aware that there are three I/O manipulators (namely std::hex, std::oct, and std::dec) provided by the standard C++. But I've always wondered why there is no std::bin manipulator in the standard library.

Note that I am not looking for workarounds, but instead want to know the historical reason(s) why no std::bin was added to the language. I am also aware of std::bitset, etc, but I want to know the reasons why it was not added to the standard, which may be documented somewhere in the old C++ docs, etc.

I think there can be some length ambiguity in printing in this form, but there may be more reasons.
rows.key_body:
<iostream> was originally modeled after the legacy C printf API lacking support for binary format. It was meant to make a safe replacement for variadic functions.

It wasn't until C++14 that the 0b prefix was adopted into C++ as the binary literal value indicator, and by that time, the critical design flaws of <iostream> were well-known. Besides that the C++11 adoption of variadic templates had already started the quest for simpler interfaces. Today <iostream> is maintained as legacy burden.

The output is now carried out using C++23 header <print> with std::print, and std::println handling standard output as well as formatted file output to std::ostream, std::ofstream, and the C API std::FILE *. The new std::formatter adds support for binary through b format argument.

On a C++20 setup <format> gives std::format — using same std::formatter — as the replacement for sprintf. So combination of std::puts, or std::fputs with std::format and std::string::c_str can temporarily fill in the place of <print>.

Otherwise the refrence implementation of <format> and <print> is the {fmt} library — compatible with C++17.

All in all, <iostream> is only being used for istream input, in modern code. If {scanlib} hits the maturity level of {fmt}, or a better implementation of C++ regexp emerges, we can finally totally retire <iostream> as deprecated. So, short answer to original question is that <iostream> is not worth more investment.
rows.title: Why is there no std::bin stream manipulator in C++?

rows.body:
I recently encountered an interesting C++ code example that compiles with Clang (-std=c++20) but fails with GCC and MSVC. The code involves operator overloading and friend function declarations.

Code Example:

#include <iostream>

template<typename T>
class Foo;

template<typename T>
Foo<T> operator+(int, const Foo<T>&);

template<typename T>
class Foo
{
public:
    Foo(const T& val) : data(val) {}
    Foo operator+(int);

    friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);

private:
    T data;
};

template<typename T>
Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int num)
{
    return Foo(this->data + num);
}

template<typename T>
Foo<T> operator+(int num, const Foo<T>& other)
{
    return Foo(other.data + num);
}

int main()
{
    Foo<int> a(1);
    auto v1 = a + 2;
    auto v2 = 2 + a;
}

Compiler Behavior: Clang (17.0.1): Works with -std=c++20

GCC (13.2): Fails with error about operator+ not being declared

MSVC (v19.38): Similar failure

GCC has an error:

<source>: In instantiation of 'class Foo<int>':
<source>:35:15:   required from here
   35 |     Foo<int> a(1);
      |               ^
<source>:15:19: error: template-id 'operator+<>' for 'Foo<int> operator+(int, const Foo<int>&)' does not match any template declaration
   15 |     friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);
      |                   ^~~~~~~~~~~
<source>:22:8: note: candidate is: 'Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int) [with T = int]'
   22 | Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int num)
      |        ^~~~~~
<source>: In instantiation of 'Foo<T> operator+(int, const Foo<T>&) [with T = int]':
<source>:37:19:   required from here
   37 |     auto v2 = 2 + a;
      |                   ^
<source>:30:22: error: 'int Foo<int>::data' is private within this context
   30 |     return Foo(other.data + num);
      |                ~~~~~~^~~~
<source>:18:7: note: declared private here
   18 |     T data;
      |       ^~~~

Workaround: Swapping the order of operator declarations inside the class makes it work:

template<typename T>
class Foo
{
public:
    Foo(const T& val) : data(val) {}
    friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);
    Foo operator+(int);

private:
    T data;
};
rows.key_body: it seems to be that Foo + operater wasn't instantiated and thus never properly functions for the call. where as you're workaround gives a way to deduce and is actually a template now, where as it can't use the operator as a template and thus never functions due to it never doing anything since operator itself does not provide template functionality.
rows.title: Why does this C++ operator overloading code work in Clang but not GCC/MSVC with C++20?

rows.body:
struct foo {
    const int bar;
};

struct foo {
    const int *bar;
}

Do the 2 const qualifiers have any role?
rows.key_body:
In structs as elsewhere,

  • const int bar (aka int const bar) means that bar is a constant int. Once initialized, the object can't be modified directly.
  • int * const bar means that bar is a constant pointer to an int. Once initialized, the object can't be modified directly.
  • const int * bar (aka int const * bar) means that bar is a pointer to a constant int object. bar isn't constant and can be modified. But the pointer can't be used to modify the int object to which it points.
  • const int * const bar (aka int const * const bar) means that bar is a constant pointer to a constant int object. In this situation, the pointer is constant, and it can't be used to modify the int object to which it points.

(The spiral rule can be used to "decipher" the meaning of a declaration. If there's nothing that follows the name being declared, it simplifies to reading from back to front.)

This is easy to check!

#include <stdio.h>

struct Foo {
    const int bar;  // `bar` is a constant `int`
};

int main( void ) {
   struct Foo foo = { 123 };
   foo.bar = 456;  // error: assignment of read-only member 'bar'
   printf( "%d\n", foo.bar );
}

Changing to a pointer makes no difference:

#include <stdio.h>

struct Foo {
    int * const bar;  // `bar` is a constant pointer to an `int`
};

int main( void ) {
   int i = 123;
   int j = 456;
   struct Foo foo = { &i };
   foo.bar = &j;        // error: assignment of read-only member 'bar'
   *( foo.bar ) = 789;  // ok
   printf( "%d\n", *( foo.bar ) );
}

In your second snippet, it's not bar that's constant but *bar.

#include <stdio.h>

struct Foo {
    const int * bar;  // `bar` is a pointer to a constant `int`
};

int main( void ) {
   int i = 123;
   int j = 456;
   struct Foo foo = { &i };
   foo.bar = &j;        // ok
   *( foo.bar ) = 789;  // error: assignment of read-only location '*foo.bar'
   printf( "%d\n", *( foo.bar ) );
}

Finally, both the pointer and that to which it points are constant in the following snippet:

#include <stdio.h>

struct Foo {
    const int * const bar;  // `bar` is a constant pointer to a constant `int`
};

int main( void ) {
   int i = 123;
   int j = 456;
   struct Foo foo = { &i };
   foo.bar = &j;        // error: assignment of read-only member 'bar'
   *( foo.bar ) = 789;  // error: assignment of read-only location '*foo.bar'
   printf( "%d\n", *( foo.bar ) );
}
rows.title: Does a const qualifier inside a struct member declaration do anything?

By including the following <intent> element within the <queries> tag in the AndroidManifest.xml file, I can access a list of all installed apps on a device:

<queries>
    <intent>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
    </intent>
</queries>

Since most Android apps have a launcher activity, doing the following returns all the apps installed in an android device:

getPackageManager().queryIntentActivities(new Intent(Intent.ACTION_MAIN), PackageManager.MATCH_ALL)

Isn't this a potential privacy loophole and almost equivalent to the very sensitive QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES permission? I see so many apps with this intent element under the queries element in their manifest files.
rows.key_body:
doing the following returns all the apps installed in an android device:

FWIW, that code returns activities, not apps.

Isn't this a potential privacy loophole and almost equivalent to the very sensitive QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES permission?

Yes, which is why I and others wrote about this years ago.

Bear in mind that Google (and other app distributors) could penalize developers for having overly-broad <queries> requests.

rows.body:
Consider the following HTML snippet:

foo <input type="text" value="bar"> 
<select>
  <option>baz</option>
</select> qux

You see "foo bar baz qux" rendered. But, in Firefox at least, if you select the whole thing and copy and paste it into another program, the text in the controls gets skipped, so all that pastes is "foo qux".

How can I make the entire string "foo bar baz qux" paste instead, short of using JavaScript to construct the entire clipboard contents from scratch?
rows.key_body:
(Edit: since Kaiido fixed "sneaking" text content nodes inside elements for Firefox to copy (through attribute or real text child) so it now supports even <select>, that answer could probably be the best option, however arcane it may seem.)

Not a "pretty" approach, but somewhat pragmatic, and quite obvious:

Mirror values beside their inputs

Instead of messing with the copy event and constructing the entire clipboard contents from scratch in JS, I'd just be frank and kept the value mirrored along respective elements for copy to pick, visually hidden, and also hidden from screen readers.

Minimal POC that does not bother to do anything special; uses capturing listener on entire document that watches for input events and single "onload" loop that sets up what is in the HTML from the start. Mirrored values are displayed here just for clarity:

function mirrorValueForCopy(event) {
  const tgt = event.target;
  let prev = tgt.previousElementSibling;
  if (prev && prev.hasAttribute('data-mirror')) {
    prev.textContent = tgt.value;
  } else {
    tgt.insertAdjacentHTML(
      'beforebegin',
      `<mark data-mirror aria-hidden="true">${tgt.value}</mark>`
    );
  }
}
document.documentElement.addEventListener('input', mirrorValueForCopy, true);
document.querySelectorAll('input,select').forEach(i => mirrorValueForCopy({
  target: i
}))
[data-mirror] {
  font-size: .7rem;
  /* Use 0 for real hiding, or, you know, clip, position, whatever. */
}
foo
<input value="bar" id="a">
<select>
  <option>baz</option>
  <option>gazonk</option>
</select>
qux

Caveats and details to handle in real-world

  • Obviously, not suitable for HTML/CSS structure that depends on the exact DOM order, sibling index and so on.
  • For brevity omitted any attempt to not making duplicate clipboard content in Chromium.
  • For brevity omitted any mutation observer that would set up mirror for newly appended inputs that had not been interacted with.
  • Also no early return filter for 'input' emitters that Firefox can copy values from natively (if any).

Addendum: using the "real" texts as pseudo-label overlays

The mechanism somewhat asks what about making these duplicates appear like the actual input content? I did some testing, and it could work to some extent, but brings probably more new problems than it solves. POC:

function mirrorValueForCopy(event) {
  const tgt = event.target;
  if (tgt.matches('[type="checkbox"],[type="radio"]')) return;
  let prev = tgt.previousElementSibling;
  if (prev && prev.hasAttribute('data-mirror')) {
    prev.textContent = tgt.value;
  } else {
    tgt.insertAdjacentHTML(
      'beforebegin',
      `<mark data-mirror aria-hidden="true">${tgt.value}</mark>`
    );
  }
}
document.documentElement.addEventListener('input', mirrorValueForCopy, true);
document.querySelectorAll('input:not([type="checkbox"],[type="radio"]),select').forEach(i => mirrorValueForCopy({
  target: i
}))
[data-mirror] {
  position: absolute;
  &:has(+ :focus) {
    z-index: -1;
  }
  pointer-events: none;
  white-space: pre;
}
<label>
 <input type="checkbox" id="nl2space" checked>
 single line clipboard
</label>
<p oncopy="
  if(!nl2space.checked){return};
  event.clipboardData.setData(
   'text/plain',
    document.getSelection().toString().replaceAll(/\r\n|\r|\n/g,' ')
  );
  event.preventDefault();
">
  foo
  <input value="bar">
  <select>
    <option>baz</option>
    <option>gazonk</option>
  </select>
  qux
</p>

<textarea placeholder="try here"></textarea>.

The problems and caveats:

  • Disabled pointer-events so the click reaches the actual input/select.
  • While the floating pseudo-labels could be actual labels, it would lose the position information, and would not open the select.
  • Firefox tends to add newlines whenever the selection contains anything positioned (it seems). That's why the oncopy cleaner there.
  • Arguably, having the oncopy handler is pretty close to the reconstructing clipboard content what we wanted to avoid, but at least there still is no treewalker involved.
rows.title: Make text in form controls copy along with regular text in browsers

I noticed that modern C compilers typically use push instructions to save caller-saved registers, rather than explicit mov + sub sequences. However, based on llvm-mca simulations, the mov approach appears more efficient in some cases. Why is this?

On Skylake, push shows a clear dependency chain in llvm-mca. I also tested this on AMD’s Zen 5 (znver5), where push performance approaches mov but remains slower, with the same dependency chain behavior.

I analyzed two ways to save caller-saved registers:

  1. push sequence: 12x push instructions.
  2. mov sequence: 12x mov to stack + 1x sub rsp, 96.

Using llvm-mca (Skylake model), the mov version shows better throughput:

  • uOps: 36 (push) vs 13 (mov).

Question: Possible reasons I considered:

  1. Code size: push is more compact (1 byte vs ~4 bytes for mov with offset).
  2. Hardware optimizations: Do real CPUs handle push better? (Probably stack engine optimization, but I can't find information about it)
  3. Compiler heuristics: Is push chosen for legacy compatibility or edge cases?
rows.key_body:
llvm-mca's model is wrong. Intel since Pentium-M, and AMD since K10, have a "stack engine" which handles offsets to RSP from stack ops like push/pop and call/ret, so they can be single uop and not have a dependency chain through the stack pointer, rSP. -march=k8 and -march=nocona (Pentium 4) are the only mainstream x86-64 without a stack engine, and they're so old they're irrelevant for -mtune=generic.

See What is the stack engine in the Sandybridge microarchitecture? and Agner Fog's microarch guide, https://agner.org/optimize/ . For accurate instruction uop counts and throughput/latency, see https://uops.info/. If you click on a number in its table, you can see the loops that were profiled with nanobench to give that result, and the perf counter results. Great resource, thanks to @AndreasAbel for creating it. (although it hasn't been updated for Zen 5 or for Intel newer than Alder Lake :/)

https://uica.uops.info/ is a loop analyzer for Intel SnB-family up to Ice Lake, like LLVM-MCA except accurate. It uses uop data from uops.info, and a model of the front-end issue and uop-to-port allocation patterns that Intel CPUs use, among other things. Andreas wrote a paper about it, showing it predicts performance more accurately than IACA or LLVM-MCA.

With -m32 -mtune=pentium3 you should see GCC avoiding push/pop, including for passing args with -maccumulate-outgoing-args. Maybe also with Clang/LLVM, but it's a newer compiler that never needed to care about tuning for some really old CPUs.

I'm not sure when Silvermont-family got a stack engine, but almost certainly push is efficient on modern E-cores descended from Silvermont. First-gen Silvermont ran push as a single uop for both integer pipes, and pop as 2 uops, so maybe it didn't have a stack engine, but its overall low throughput made it not a big problem. Goldmont, second-gen Silvermont-family, has single-uop pop reg. And it does limited mov-elimination in rename, so probably they're also eliminating RSP updates, too.

Fun fact: Alder Lake P-cores (Golden Cove) eliminate add/sub reg, small-immediate in general, but separate from the stack engine even for RSP so you still need stack-sync uops. For the general mechanism that works on add/sub/inc/dec, no extra sync uop is needed when reading the value, though. (https://chipsandcheese.com/i/149874006/rename-and-allocate-feeding-the-backend talks about it, and has a table for Lion Cove and Redwood Cove vs. Zen 5.)

A stack-sync uop is needed when instructions like mov rbp, rsp follow some stack ops, to update the back-end with the actual RSP value and zero out the offset in the renamer. Any instruction which reads RSP explicitly has this effect when the stack engine offset is non-zero, like mov eax, [rsp+8]. Also if the offset gets too high; apparently it's signed 8-bit in P-M, so if you were really running push in a loop like you're asking LLVM-MCA to analyze, you'd expect 1 in 32 push instructions to effectively be multi-uop. (Assuming it's still only an 8-bit offset, but that makes sense; most use-cases will use sub rsp, imm at some point, although a long chain of pushes and calls is plausible possible.)

On function entry, unless it was a jmp tailcall, the last instruction was call so the stack-engine offset is already non-zero. So there's no downside to using push even if we are going to allocate some stack space later with sub rsp, 24 or something. (In a function that starts with push rbp / mov rbp, rsp, doing more pushes after that will normally require a stack-sync uop at some point, but that's usually fine and worth it for the code-size advantage of push. Function prologues shouldn't run super often; small hot functions should get inlined in most cases, especially with -flto for cross-file inlining.)

I even used pop instead of lodsd to optimize a code-golf size+performance BigInt Fibonacci problem. I profiled it with performance counters on my i7-6700k Skylake, so I'm 100% certain the stack engine exists and works as intended to make pop fast and single-uop.

The one advantage to sub rsp, imm + mov-stores would be smaller stack-unwind metadata since RSP only moves once, so only one entry. So smaller executables and libraries. But that's metadata, separate from .text, so it doesn't even help with load times or with I-cache or iTLB footprint. Using RBP as a frame pointer also allows smaller stack-unwind metadata, but also isn't worth it when we care about speed.

You're correct that push being a 1 or 2 byte instruction is a nice advantage.
rows.title: Why do C compilers still prefer PUSH over MOV for saving registers, even when MOV appears faster in llvm-mca?

I ran into the same issue recently on a previously stable app, and it turned out to be related to the latest bcrypt release. A change in behavior between passlib and bcrypt seems to have caused problems even when the input was well under the 72-byte limit.

What solved it for me was pinning bcrypt to version 4.3.0, instead of allowing the upgrade to 5.0.0 (released on 2025-09-25). After making that change, the errors stopped.

For example, in Python you can update requirements.txt from:

bcrypt

to:

bcrypt==4.3.0

This ensures your environment uses the last known stable version. If you’re working with another stack (React, FastAPI, etc.), the same principle applies — make sure you’re not pulling in bcrypt 5.0.0 until compatibility issues are resolved.

rows.body:
I'm building a browser-based FPS game and I want to include gamepad/xbox controller support.

The common method to detect gamepad button presses is to just use polling with requestAnimationFrame:

function poll() {
  let gamepads = navigator.getGamepads();
  if (gamepads.length > 0) {
    let gamepad = gamepads[0];
    if (gamepad.buttons[0].pressed) {
      console.log("Button 'A' pressed!");
    }
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(poll);
}
poll();

The problem with this method is that, if there is a large drop in framerate (such as a sudden freeze), the user will be able to press a button once or multiple times, which will go undetected while the freeze happens. This doesn't just happen with low framerates either. It happens even on devices with high framerates. I notice it especially when I spam a button and the script only detects one or two presses.

How do I detect gamepad button presses as an event listener rather than polling, since that would be more accurate?
rows.key_body:
The problem isn't really requestAnimationFrame() itself. The Gamepad API only gives you the current button state, not a history of presses that happened between checks.

For example, if the game freezes for half a second and the player presses and releases A during that time, the next check will see the button as released. There's no way to tell that it was pressed.

One possible improvement is to poll on a timer rather than waiting for each animation frame.

let wasPressed = false;

function checkInput() {
  const gamepad = navigator.getGamepads()[0];

  if (!gamepad) {
    wasPressed = false;
    return;
  }

  const pressed = gamepad.buttons[0].pressed;

  if (pressed && !wasPressed) {
    console.log("A pressed");
  }

  wasPressed = pressed;
}

setInterval(checkInput, 10);

This checks the controller approximately every 10 milliseconds instead of waiting for the next animation frame. It may help when rendering slows down, although the browser isn't guaranteed to run the interval exactly on time.

If the main JavaScript thread freezes, the interval stops running too. Any press-and-release cycle that happens entirely during that freeze can still be missed.

So you can reduce missed inputs by keeping the main thread responsive and polling frequently, but you can't guarantee detection of every button press using the standard Gamepad API. There is no standard buttondown or buttoup event for gamepad buttons.
rows.title: How do I accurately detect gamepad button presses in JavaScript?

rows.body:
Having this regex pattern (in c#):

^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}$

this string will match:

11/10/25 17:22:31

but this one will not (it just has an added "X")

X11/10/25 17:22:31

neither will this one:

11/10/25 X17:22:31

Is there any way to find out, when a string does not match the pattern, what parts of the strings are the ones making it not match? (ie. find the characters that, if removed, would make the regex match) So in this case, how to find the "X"?

Why I want this: I am reading a bunch of text files where every line should match a pattern. But I have found out that in many cases, the file seems somehow corrupted and some character is randomly added somewhere in some of the lines, making it not match the regex. As of now, I am just ignoring those strings as non-valid, but I am trying to find if a string is not making a match just because a single "rogue" char somewhere, so that just removing this char, the regex will match the pattern and I can then consider it valid. Hope this explanation makes sense...
rows.key_body:
Even if your question has been closed for obscure reasons, I want to say: it's a very interesting question about regex!

Most of the time, the goal of a validation regex is build to say if a string is conform to a format. It's a binary choice and doesn't give you more informations about where the format isn't conform in the string.

To find where the pattern fails, you have to build an always successful pattern where all characters on the right are optional. And to know at which character the pattern fails, you have to be able to know, where is the last successful character. To do that, you need to enclose each character into an optional capture group.

These optional capture groups have to be nested.

Example:

Your validation pattern is:

^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}$

You have to write it like that:

^(\d(\d(/(\d(\d(/(\d(\d( (\d(\d(:(\d(\d(:(\d(\d($)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?

This way, you only have to check what capturing groups exist to know where the pattern fails. Obviously, C# gives you the offset of each capture group.

If you are interested on particular positions in the string, don't forget to use named capturing groups.
rows.title: How to find what characters in a string are making it to not match a regex pattern?

While writing a library that will be shared between programs compiled under GCC 14.2.0 for X86 and ARM 6.22 for Cortex-M, I came upon a discrepancy between how the two compilers handle the recursive lambda capture when using the new 'this auto &&' deduced 'this' feature.

Here is the code:

/* Compiled with --std=c++23 option */

struct Foo
{
  int s = 1 ;

  void zook (void)
    {
      auto f_ok = [ & s = s ] (this auto && f , int x) -> void // ok
        {
          if (x < 10) f (x + s) ;
        } ;

      auto f_bad = [ & ] (this auto && f , int x) -> void // error: invalid use of non-static data member 'Foo::s'
        {
          if (x < 10) f (x + s) ;
        } ;

      f_ok  (1) ;
      f_bad (1) ;
    }
} ;

The 'f_ok' lambda with the explicit reference capture of the 's' variable works fine.

The 'f_bad' lambda, which uses '&', should capture the 's' variable but generates a compiler error as shown in the code comments when compiled using GCC.

The ARM compiler accepts both versions and generates the same binary, but the GCC compiler complains for the 'f_bad' version.

I spend some time going deep into the woods of the C++ specification and was unable to determine what the standard says about this particular case.

I suspect at this point that there is a compiler bug in GCC.

In order to be certain, I need to know what the C++23 standard specifies regarding lambda captures under these conditions.

If anybody can shed some light on this, and/or perhaps point to the relevant part of the specification, I would appreciate it.
rows.key_body:
When you capture this, explicitly or implicitly ([this]{...} or [&]{...}), it's as if your lambda is a hidden method on the object. When you capture an explicit this ([](this auto &&f) {...}), your lambda function is actually a method on the lambda, not the original object. A method can only be a method of a single object, so GCC is correct.

Note: you can capture both the object and the lambda, as in [&obj=*this](this auto &&lambda){...} and even access private fields of obj.
rows.title: Need clarification on how to capture by reference in C++ recursive lambda

I am working on a ultra low latency ring buffer in C++20 on an Intel Ice Lake (x86_64) architecture. I am trying to optimize the producer thread's throughput by minimizing cache pollution when writing large blocks of telemetry data, before signaling the consumer thread via a std::atomic<uint64_64> sequence counter.

Normally, the release-store sequence looks like this:

// thread 1 (Producer)
std::memcpy(shared_buffer, local_data, 64); // Write 64 bytes
ring_buffer_tail.store(new_tail, std::memory_order_release);

I replaced the standard std::memcpy with AVX-512 non-temporal vector stores (_mm512_stream_si512) to bypass the L1/L2 caches and write directly to main memory (Write-Combining memory type behavior).

// optimized thread 1 (Producer)
_mm512_stream_si512(reinterpret_block, vector_data); // Non-temporal store
ring_buffer_tail.store(new_tail, std::memory_order_release);

std::memory_order_release makes sure that all previous writes (including the non-temporal vector store) are visible to another thread once that thread acquires the atomic variable.

On x86_64, standard atomic stores are compiled into a simple MOV instruction because the hardware memory model is strongly ordered (Total Store Order / TSO).

BUT, during high-frequency micro-benchmarking using hardware performance counters (perf), I noticed a massive 300-cycle stall on the very next local, completely unrelated relaxed load (std::memory_order_relaxed) executed by the same producer thread.

If I switch back to standard std::memcpy, the stall completely disappears.

Does the x86 MOV instruction used by std::memory_order_release force a partial or full drain of the WC Buffers to satisfy C++ release semantics, or does the stall occur because a subsequent std::memory_order_relaxed load triggers an internal CPU pipeline flush due to a false memory dependency alias across the Store Buffer and Fill Buffer boundaries?
rows.key_body: no, the standard x86 MOV instruction does not force a drain of the Line Fill Buffers/Write-Combining buffers, but that is why your producer thread is stalling
rows.title: Shifting an atomic store to a non-temporal vector instruction bypass the CPU's Store Buffer forwarding, causing a relaxed load to stall

rows.body:
Here's the test code:

#include <concepts>

template<typename T>
concept Printable = requires(T obj) {
    { obj.print() } -> std::same_as<void>;
};

template<Printable T>
void func(const T& obj)
{
    obj.print();
}

class Foo
{
private:
    void print() const { /* std::cout << "Foo" << std::endl; */ }

public:
    void bar() {
        static_assert(Printable<Foo>);
        func(*this);
    }
};

print() is a private member of Foo, so Foo shouldn't satisfy the concept Printable. But within bar(), print() is accessible, and it seems it mislead GCC to believe Foo satisfies Printable in the static_assert.
Additionally, it seems to fix/cache the value of Printable<Foo> to true, so in the line below, func(*this), GCC incorrectly tries to instanciate func<Foo> (believing Foo does satisfy Printable) then complains that print() is private.

MSVC, on the other hand, report an error at static_assert because of Foo not satisfying Printable

clang 20.1.0 (the latest on godbolt as I'm writing this question) has the same behavior as GCC, but the trunk build agrees with MSVC.

Godbolt link with the latest versions of compilers at the time of writing this question

Are GCC and non-trunk versions of clang in the wrong? Or perhaps did I invoke some undefined behavior?
rows.key_body:
A concept is a named constraint. Your concept is

template<typename T>
concept Printable = requires(T obj) {
    { obj.print() } -> std::same_as<void>;
};

So Printable means that obj.print() can be called. Since print() is private in your example and you expose it via another method, it seems to be a bug, as the expectation is to be able to call the print() method directly and you cannot do an obj.print().
rows.title: Is this concept satisfaction a bug in GCC or did I invoke undefined behavior?

rows.body:
I have a following embedded system optimization case (simplified).

int main() {
  while (1) { 
    // Do something
    if (unrecoverable_error) {  
      __breakpoint(); 
      while(1); 
    }
  } 
}

If the while (1); statement is replaced by return 0, the compiler invokes all the destructors due upon exit from main, (and for that matter generates the destructor code bloat) - both for main-local and global, even if the crt0 ultimately traps the CPU in a while(1); loop after all.

Thus, there is an advantage to judiciously use while(1); if one wants the system to intentionally hang.

Statically analyzing the code with -fanalyzer leads to (obvious) infinite loop error/warning.

How does one annotate that a specific instance of the infinite loop is indeed intentional?

I don't want to disable the infinite loop detection entirely (as it is possible that other parts of the code may contain bugs that lead to non-trivial infinite loops).
rows.key_body:
Infinite loops without side effects are generally considered as undefined behavior in C++ (Some exceptions in the newest draft are given in the comments of the question).

According to the latest draft, reading from a volatile object is considered a side effect.

Therefore you might replace the while(1); statement with

volatile int dummy = 1;
while (1) { // I do not know if side effect in control statement counts
    if (!dummy)
        break;
}
rows.title: Annotating intentional infinite loop to satisfy "-fanalyzer"

rows.body:
JEP 455 introduced Primitive Types in Patterns, instanceof, and switch as a preview feature in JDK 23. It continues as a preview feature in JDK 24 and 25, so the feature is not detailed in the Java Language Specification.

The JEP describes "safety of conversions", where certain pairs of types are unconditionally exact, meaning no runtime checks are required. For other pairs, a runtime test is necessary to determine if a conversion can be made without loss of information.

For example:

int x = getValue();  // Which returns 42

switch (x) {
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
}

The runtime check verifies that 42 will fit in a byte and matches, printing 'byte'.

If we change the order of the cases:

switch (x) {
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This will result in a compiler error because the int case now dominates the byte case.

Quoting from the Java Language Specification (where pattern dominance is defined),

A switch label in a switch block is said to be dominated if for every value that it applies to, it can be determined that one of the preceding switch labels would also apply.

So far, everything makes sense.

However, if we change the case for int to use the wrapper class Integer:

switch (x) {
  case Integer -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This code will compile without an error, and the result will be 'int'.

The compiler is clearly autoboxing the int to an Integer and matching the first case.

What I can't understand is why the compiler allows this, since the Integer case is still dominating the byte case. Any value that will match for a byte will also match for a boxed Integer.

JEP 507, the latest version states:

Furthermore, boxing conversions and widening reference conversions are unconditionally exact.

However, that still does not explain why the compiler is not rejecting this because of pattern dominance.

Just to be clear, all the examples use the same line, int x = getValue();, where getValue() returns 42.
rows.key_body:
Domination is a relationship between the patterns themselves. The selector expression does not matter.

(Whether or not the type of the selector expression should be considered for determining dominance is another matter, and outside of the scope of this answer.)

As Jon Skeet said in the comments,

"Any value that will match for a byte will also match for a boxed Integer." Is that actually the case? What about a boxed Byte?

From the preview spec, the Integer pattern does not dominate the byte pattern. The relevant quotes are

(14.11.1)

A case label with a case pattern q is dominated if there is a preceding unguarded case label in the switch block with a case pattern p, and p dominates q

(14.30.3)

A pattern p dominates a type pattern that declares a pattern variable of type T if p is unconditional for T.

A type pattern that declares a pattern variable of a type S is unconditional for a type T if there is a testing conversion that is unconditionally exact (5.7.2) from |T| to |S|.

None of these definitions refer to the selector expression of the switch.

For this case, we can substitute Integer for "S" and byte for "T" into the last quote, and show that there is no testing conversion that is unconditionally exact from byte to Integer.

The unconditionally exact testing conversions are (5.7.2):

  • an identity conversion
  • an exact widening primitive conversion
  • a widening reference conversion
  • a boxing conversion
  • a boxing conversion followed by a widening reference conversion

To convert from byte to Integer, we need an (exact) widening primitive conversion followed by a boxing conversion, which is not in the above list.
rows.title: Primitive types in patterns: why doesn't Integer dominate byte?

rows.body:
I'm trying to create a static extension method that can be used with any enum type in C#. I want to be able to call this method on any enum value.

However, since extension methods are defined for specific types, I'm unsure how to create a generic extension method that applies to all enums. Is there a way to do this using extension blocks?

Now I could define a method only for the specific enum:

extension(MyEnum)
{
     public static Direction Random => Enum.GetValues<MyEnum>().Choice();
}

But I want something like this:

extension<T>() where T : Enum
{
    public static T Random => Enum.GetValues<T>().Choice();
}
rows.key_body:
Your syntax and generic constraints are both slightly off:

  • You still need to put the type you're extending within the parentheses, so extension<T>(T)
  • You need to constrain T to be a non-nullable value type as well (in order to call Enum.GetValues<T>(), so where T : struct, Enum

This compiles (assuming a suitable Choice method):

public static class Extensions
{
    extension<T>(T) where T : struct, Enum
    {
        public static T Random => Enum.GetValues<T>().Choice();
    }
}

I'd recommend making this a method rather than a property though.
rows.title: How can I create a static extension method for all Enum types?

rows.body:
When a module needs to include a header, the following usually doesn't work, since the header contents get attached to the module: (with function names getting mangled to include the module name, etc)

export module A;
#include <iostream> // Wrong

Including in the global module fragment does work, as it attaches the header contents to the global module:

module;
#include <iostream>
export module A;

Including in an extern "C++" block also seems to work:

export module A;
extern "C++"
{
    #include <iostream>
}

Some compilers warn about the latter, but that seems to be a generic warning for includes, that fails to check for extern "C++" above the include.

Is there any difference between the last two snippets? Other than the warnings, is there any reason to prefer one or the other?

(Note, I'm tagging c++20 because this is the version that introduced modules. If the answer is different for newer standards, I want the answer for the latest standard, not for C++20.)
rows.key_body:
Certainly you should prefer the actual global module fragment over the emulation thereof, for several reasons:

  1. #include of certain header files may get transformed into import, which must appear immediately after the module declaration (or else in the global module fragment).
  2. If an #include is not so translated, the file included might contain an import which would be so restricted.
  3. Declarations in the global module fragment are discarded if they are not directly used, so that they do not require space in the compiled module interface and time in importers. (Obviously you might want to provide access to more of the interface, but that would involve export using declarations that would prevent the discarding anyway.)
  4. Build systems try to optimize scanning module files to find dependencies, and #includes later would defeat that.
rows.title: Is there any difference between the global module fragment and the `extern "C++"` blocks?

XQueryKeymap only captures key states at the exact microsecond the function executes.

You should open the display once outside the loop and dramatically lower the usleep interval (e.g., to 10–20 milliseconds) so you don't miss the physical keypresses.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <X11/Xlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    Display *display = XOpenDisplay(NULL);
    if (!display) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open X display\n");
        return 1;
    }

    char keys_return[32];

    while(1) {
        XQueryKeymap(display, keys_return);
        
        int key_pressed = 0;
        for(int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
            if (keys_return[i] != 0) {
                key_pressed = 1;
                break;
            }
        }

        if (key_pressed) {
            putchar('[');
            for(int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
                printf("%d ", (unsigned char)keys_return[i]);
            }
            printf("]\n");
        }

        usleep(10000); 
    }

    XCloseDisplay(display);

rows.body:
I am going through "C++ Primer", and it is mentioned that for the following code:

double dval = 3.14;
const int &ri = dval; //Bind a const int to a plain double object.

The transformation of the code will be:

const int temp = dval; //Create a temporary const int from the double
const int &ri = temp;  //bind ri to that temporary

So, if I modify dval, say I set it to dval = 3.0, since ri will be bound to the temporary object, the changed value will not be reflected.

Wouldn't this cause a lot of subtle bugs? Why is such a thing allowed? It is not intuitive as a reference.
rows.key_body:
Wouldn't this cause a lot of subtle bugs

It can cause bugs, but there are probably not a lot of them in the wild.

and why such a thing is allowed as it is not intuitive as a reference?

To allow for binding references to prvalues to not have to copy them.

Take john's example in the comments:

void foo(const int& ri);

foo(3.14159);

In practice, there's little risk here. You call the function and in most scenarios, the value ri references is not expected to change during the call.

If you actually do have a situation where another function may change the referenced value, you can constrain your function to not allow for anything but the exact type you want to bind a reference to to avoid the temporary being created:

void foo(std::same_as<int> auto const& ri);

In reality, most compilers (MSVC with /W2 or higher and icx, clang and gcc with -Wfloat-conversion) are able to warn for this kind of mistake, further minimizing the risk for bugs.
rows.title: C++ temporary objects and constant reference

rows.body:
In the talk "Taking a Byte Out of C++ - Avoiding Punning by Starting Lifetimes - Robert Leahy - CppCon 2022", the presenter shows the following code as a pre-C++23 alternative to std::start_lifetime_as:

template<typename T> 
[[nodiscard]]
T* start_lifetime_as(void* mem) noexcept{
    auto bytes = new (mem) unsigned char[sizeof(T)];
    auto ptr = reinterpret_cast<T*>(bytes); 
    (void)*ptr; 
    return ptr; 
}

The first line of this function is valid. It's starting a new lifetime of an array of bytes in the location of memory where mem is pointing at. Whatever was in mem (i.e. some type U) is no longer valid unless we use std::launder to access the memory there (as far as I understand, and this is explicitly said in the talk in a later example).

On the second line, we reinterpret_cast<T*>(bytes), which while I understand doing a reinterpret_cast is in itself not UB here, doing anything with that object would appear to be UB. The lifetime of object T has not started yet. Lifetimes of objects can't be started by reinterpret_cast, AFAIK.

On the third line, I have no clue why it is necessary. Even taking the previous lines at face value, the presenter towards the end starts talking about how they could have used std::launder instead, but because they didn't introduce std::launder yet and it would "be a pretty weird" use of std::launder, they decided not to use it here.

First, I don't understand how std::launder could be used. The object T still has not been created yet, and second why does de-referencing a void casting seem to "create" the object lifetime, as implied by the author?

I do understand type T must be an "implicit lifetime type" to work here, but I don't know how that changes the situation with respect to UB, if at all.
rows.key_body:
The code leans on one C++20 feature it never names: implicit object creation (P0593).

[intro.object]/10: "An operation that begins the lifetime of an array of unsigned char or std::byte implicitly creates objects within the region of storage occupied by the array" — and that operation creates implicit-lifetime objects "if doing so would result in the program having defined behavior."

That clause is the trick. The abstract machine can retroactively create implicit-lifetime objects, choosing whatever set keeps your program defined. No constructor runs; the object just takes on the bytes already sitting there. Exactly what you want for bytes off a socket or malloc.

new (mem) unsigned char[sizeof(T)] begins the array's lifetime, so it's one of those creating operations. It'll produce a T there only if something later needs one, and only if T is implicit-lifetime.

reinterpret_cast<T*>(bytes) starts no lifetime, right. Pure pointer math.

(void)*ptr; is the line that matters. *ptr is a T glvalue, and indirection needs a real T at that address to be defined. That's the "need" that forces line 1 to create the T — so its lifetime counts from there and ptr points to it. Drop the line and nothing demands a T, so you'd return a pointer to nothing. It isn't constructing anything; it's supplying the well-definedness the creation rule keys off. Hence the "the dereference creates it" feeling.

Same reason T has to be implicit-lifetime: that rule only ever creates those types. Otherwise *ptr designates nothing and it's UB.

std::launder wouldn't help — it doesn't create objects, it just defeats the optimiser's assumptions about what's at an address. The reinterpret_cast pointer already designates the T once line 3 forces it to exist. launder is for recovering a pointer the compiler thinks is stale, not this.

Caveats if you copy it: mem sized and aligned for T, T implicit-lifetime, value is whatever the bytes already hold. C++23's std::start_lifetime_as does all this for you.
rows.title: Why is the pre-C++23 start_lifetime_as() function described in "Taking A byte out of C++" not exhibiting Undefined Behavior?

rows.body:
I’m facing a design issue in a multithreaded C++ program related to safely shutting down threads. Here’s the problem: My main program starts multiple threads. During shutdown, I call join() on each thread to wait for them to finish properly. However, while the program is stuck inside join(), an interrupt signal (e.g., SIGINT from Ctrl+C) can arrive. The signal handler immediately tries to stop all threads and also tries to join() again, or perform unsafe cleanup. This causes undefined behavior, because: There’s no way to know if a thread is already inside join(). join() is a blocking the call — if interrupted halfway, it’s unclear what the state of the thread object is. Double-joining a thread or touching the thread incorrectly can lead to crashes or deadlocks. I thought about sleeping for a short time instead of joining immediately, but that doesn't solve the fundamental race condition between: The main thread trying to join() The signal handler trying to "force stop"

My questions: How to properly design thread shutdown when an interrupt might arrive during join()? How to avoid unsafe behavior if a signal arrives during join()?

Important notes:

The signal handler currently calls _Exit(1) after trying to stop everything, which kills the program immediately (bad - this is how they implemented it for years, no clean shutdown).

I want to move toward a safer design any solutions?
rows.key_body: Signals are an ancient Unix API. They're not really compatible with multi-threaded programs. Hence, the best idea is to block signal delivery, and check for signals yourselves from a thread you have chosen for that purpose. That thread will need to do a clean shutdown in response to SIGINT.
rows.title: How to safely handle thread join when interrupt signal (SIGINT) may arrive during join()?

How to keep the selected navigation tab in sync with the current route using GoRouter?
rows.key_body:
Don't keep the index in state; read it from the current route.

class NavigationAppBar extends StatelessWidget {
  const NavigationAppBar({super.key});

  static const _paths = ['/', '/search', '/setting'];

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    final index = _paths.indexOf(GoRouterState.of(context).uri.path);

    return NavigationBar(
      selectedIndex: index == -1 ? 0 : index,
      indicatorColor: AppColors.primary,
      onDestinationSelected: (i) => context.go(_paths[i]),
      destinations: const <NavigationDestination>[
         NavigationDestination(

          icon: Icon(Icons.home_outlined),

          icon: Icon(Icons.settings_outlined),
          label: 'Setting',
        ),

Cause:
Each of your screens has its own NavigationAppBar. When context.go(...) opens a new page, a new bar is created, so currentPageIndex starts at 0 again.

I’m using Expo Router with NativeWind v5 (Tailwind CSS v4). My design tokens are defined once in global.css using @theme:

@import "tailwindcss/theme.css" layer(theme);
@import "tailwindcss/preflight.css" layer(base);
@import "tailwindcss/utilities.css";
@import "nativewind/theme";

@theme {
  --color-primary: #081126;
  --color-accent: #ea7a53;
  --color-background: #fff9e3;
  /* ... */
}

In components I can use these with className="bg-accent". But Tabs from expo-router doesn’t accept className; it is styled through screenOptions style objects, which need real values:

<Tabs
  screenOptions={{
    headerShown: false,
    tabBarStyle: {
      position: "absolute",
      bottom: 25,
      left: 20,
      right: 20,
      elevation: 0,
      backgroundColor: /* I want to use --color-primary here */
    },
  }}
>
  {tabs.map((tab) => (
    <Tabs.Screen
      key={tab.name}
      name={tab.name}
      options={{
        tabBarIcon: ({ color }) => (
          <Ionicons name={tab.icon} size={32} color={/* --color-accent */} />
        ),
      }}
    />
  ))}
</Tabs>
rows.key_body:
This is the solution that worked for me. Someone posted it here as an answer, but it was deleted, so I’m sharing it in case it helps others.

Tabs style objects don’t accept className, but tabBarBackground renders a normal component, so a View with className works and uses the @theme color directly:


<Tabs
  screenOptions={{
    headerShown: false,
    tabBarStyle: {
      position: "absolute",
      bottom: 25,
      left: 20,
      right: 20,
      height: 72,
      elevation: 0,
    },
    tabBarBackground: () => (
      <View className="flex-1 bg-foreground rounded-4xl" />
    ),
  }}
>
  {/* your Tabs.Screen items */}
</Tabs>
rows.title: How to use @theme CSS variables from global.css in React Native Tabs tabBarStyle (NativeWind v5 / Tailwind v4) without duplicating colors?

rows.body:
Suppose I want to set a thread to use a particular real time scheduling policy with a given priority. From what I can tell, there are at least two functions that accomplish this.

From the man pages on my system:

sched_setscheduler

"The sched_setscheduler() system call sets both the scheduling policy and parameters for the thread whose ID is specified in pid."

#include <sched.h>

int sched_setscheduler(pid_t pid, int policy,
                       const struct sched_param *param);

pthread_setschedparam

"The pthread_setschedparam() function sets the scheduling policy and parameters of the thread thread."

#include <pthread.h>

int pthread_setschedparam(pthread_t thread, int policy,
                          const struct sched_param *param);

What are the differences between these two? Is there a compelling reason to use one over the other?
rows.key_body:
What are the differences between these two?

sched_setscheduler() is a system-call (wrapper), as we can know from the fact that it is documented in section 2 of the manual, if for no other reason. On Linux, the entities scheduled are native threads (not processes, contrary to another answer), identified by their native thread ids. These are the schedulable units.

pthread_setschedparam() is an ordinary-ish userspace function belonging to the Pthreads API. The entities scheduled are pthreads, which might or might not be tightly associated with native threads. When pthreads are associated with native threads, as in modern Glibc's pthreads implementation, this function relies on system interfaces such as sched_setscheduler() on the back end. It might or might not have additional pthreads-specific effects on the front end. It expects you to identify the subject (p)thread by its pthread ID.

Note well that, at least on Linux, native threads don't have to be created or managed via the Pthreads API. Whether a particular pthreads implementation creates or manages native threads at all is implementation-specific, though implementations that do so are overwhelmingly the norm these days.* On such implementations, all pthreads are closely associated with native threads, but particular native threads are not necessarily associated with pthreads.

Is there a compelling reason to use one over the other?

It is unspecified what metadata Pthreads maintains about the threads it manages, but there certainly is some. It follows that it is potentially unsafe to handle a pthreads-managed native thread via interfaces that don't account for Pthreads. And of course, on a system where Pthreads is not implemented on top of native threads, attempting to set scheduling parameters for an individual pthread via sched_setparams() will not have the intended effect.

And that may be why the Linux manual page for sched_setscheduler() says, in the VERSIONS section:

If you are using the POSIX threads API, then use pthread_setschedparam(3), pthread_getschedparam(3), and pthread_setschedprio(3), instead of the sched_*(2) system calls.

I don't know whether you would consider that compelling, but it doesn't seem like you need to be compelled so much as advised: listen to the manual. If you're using pthreads, then do not bypass its interfaces to the scheduler.

*Consider the LinuxThreads implementation of Pthreads.
rows.title: What's the difference between pthread_setschedparam and sched_setscheduler?
