I want to deploy a react router 8 app with docker. This is my package.json (showing only react router's related stuff)

{
 "scripts": {
    "build": "react-router build",
    "start": "react-router-serve ./build/server/index.js",
  },
 "dependencies": {
    "@react-router/node": "^8.4.0",
    "@react-router/serve": "^8.4.0",
    "react-router": "^8.4.0",
    "react": "^19.3.0",
    "react-dom": "^19.3.0",
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@react-router/dev": "^8.4.0",
    "@tailwindcss/vite": "^4.3.3",
    "typescript": "^7.0.2",
    "vite": "^8.3.0"
  },
}

My react-router.config.ts:

import type { Config } from '@react-router/dev/config';

export default {
  ssr: true,
} satisfies Config;

and my vite.config.ts:

import { reactRouter } from '@react-router/dev/vite';
import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
  resolve: {
    tsconfigPaths: true,
  },
  plugins: [tailwindcss(), reactRouter()],
});

Everything is very similar to the official template https://github.com/remix-run/react-router-templates/tree/main/default

Both the official template and I are omitting development dependencies from the final image. They do npm ci --omit=dev and I run npm prune --omit=dev after build. I am kinda sure that they both result in the same thing, and I am doing the latter just to save some bandwidth... Anyway, this doesn't seem to be the original problem. The broken thing is that react router docs explicitly says:

The React Router CLI comes from the @react-router/dev package. Make sure it is in your package.json devDependencies so it doesn't get deployed to your server.

But the built file imports it (!):

# build/server/index.js
...
import { index, layout, prefix, route } from "@react-router/dev/routes";
...

A quick fix will be adding @react-router/dev to dependencies rather than devDependencies (or stop pruning dev deps from final build, because build works locally when all packages are available). But this feels illegal, and I don't want to fix it that way.

Is it a bug in react-router (& is it supposed to convert routes and use another package?), or it's the documentation being misleading, or is it me using the package wrongly?

To give more context, I have many routes.ts files using this pattern:

import { index, layout, prefix, route } from '@react-router/dev/routes';

export const settings = [
  ...prefix('settings', [
    layout('./settings/layout.tsx', [
      index('./settings/page.tsx'),
      route('app', './settings/app/page.tsx'),
    ]),
  ]),
];

rows.body:
Just stumble across Why we didn't rewrite our feed handler in Rust from databento

And they say they cannot share a buffer during a loop. What would be the rust way to fix this without making copies of data? I made a minimal example

struct Source {
    id: usize,
    data: Vec<u8>,
}

impl Source {
    fn fetch_data(&self) -> Vec<u8> {
        println!("Fetching data from source {}", self.id);
        self.data.clone()
    }
}

const SPLITTER: u8 = b',';

fn process_data(chunks: &[&[u8]]) {
    println!("Processing {} chunks:", chunks.len());
    for (i, chunk) in chunks.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("  Chunk {}: {:?}", i, String::from_utf8_lossy(chunk));
    }
}

fn process_sources(sources: Vec<Source>) {
    let mut buffer: Vec<&[u8]> = Vec::new(); // allocate once

    for source in sources {
        let data: Vec<u8> = source.fetch_data();
        buffer.extend(data.split(|b| *b == SPLITTER));
        process_data(&buffer);
        buffer.clear();
    }
}

fn main() {
    let sources = vec![
        Source {
            id: 1,
            data: b"hello,world,this,is,source1".to_vec(),
        },
        Source {
            id: 2,
            data: b"foo,bar,baz".to_vec(),
        },

    ];

    process_sources(sources);
}

The error is:

error[E0597]: `data` does not live long enough
  --> src/main.rs:27:23
   |
   |         let data: Vec<u8> = source.fetch_data();
   |             ---- binding `data` declared here
   |         buffer.extend(data.split(|b| *b == SPLITTER));
   |         ------        ^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
   |         |
   |         borrow later used here
...
   |     }
   |     - `data` dropped here while still borrowed
rows.key_body:
The most idiomatic would be to avoid the allocation altogether:

fn process_data<'a, C>(chunks: C)
where
    C: IntoIterator<Item = &'a [u8]>,
{
    let mut n = 0;
    for (i, chunk) in chunks.into_iter().enumerate() {
        println!("  Chunk {}: {:?}", i, String::from_utf8_lossy(chunk));
        n += 1;
    }
    println!("Processed {n} chunks.");
}

fn process_sources(sources: Vec<Source>) {
    for source in sources {
        let data: Vec<u8> = source.fetch_data();
        process_data(data.split(|b| *b == SPLITTER));
    }
}

This doesn't allocate for the chunks at all and avoids looping over the chunks twice but doesn't let us know ahead of time how many chunks there are in total.

You can also convince the borrow checker that what you're doing is ok. The unsafe escape hatch is there to be used when necessary. Here it is additionaly wrapped in a safe wrapper which doesn't let you accidentially leak a reference like if you used data.split(…).map(|x| unsafe { &*(x as *const _) }) directly:

use buffer::Buffer;
mod buffer {
    pub struct Buffer<'pseudo, T: ?Sized> {
        data: Vec<&'pseudo T>,
    }

    impl<'pseudo, T: ?Sized> Buffer<'pseudo, T> {
        pub fn new() -> Self {
            Self { data: Vec::new() }
        }
        pub fn set<'a>(
            &'a mut self,
            items: impl IntoIterator<Item = &'a T>,
        ) -> impl std::ops::Deref<Target = [&'a T]>
        where
            T: 'a,
            'pseudo: 'a,
        {
            // make sure there are no remaining items with a different actual lifetime in the buffer
            self.data.clear();
            self.data.extend(items.into_iter().map(|x| {
                // SAFETY:
                // - `BufferView` only hands out references with the correct lifetime `'a`
                // - `BufferView` is the only way to retrieve such a reference
                // - We `clear` our internal buffer so we cannot possibly have
                //   items with two different lifetimes in the buffer at the same time
                unsafe { &*(x as *const _) }
            }));
            BufferView {
                buffer: self,
            }
        }
    }

    struct BufferView<'a, 'pseudo, T: ?Sized> {
        buffer: &'a mut Buffer<'pseudo, T>,
    }

    impl<'a, 'pseudo, T: ?Sized> std::ops::Deref for BufferView<'a, 'pseudo, T>
    where
        T: 'a,
        'pseudo: 'a,
    {
        type Target = [&'a T];
        fn deref(&self) -> &[&'a T] {
            &self.buffer.data
        }
    }
}

fn process_sources(sources: Vec<Source>) {
    let mut buffer = Buffer::new(); // allocate O(log(max(n))) times
    for source in sources {
        let data: Vec<u8> = source.fetch_data();
        let buffer = buffer.set(data.split(|b| *b == SPLITTER));
        process_data(&buffer);
    }
}
rows.title: Share buffer during a loop

rows.body:
I have a very simple C program where I am printing variables of different sizes.

#include <stdio.h>

unsigned int long long a;
unsigned int c;

int main() {
    a = 0x1111111122222222;
    c = 0x33333333;
    printf("Sizes: %zu %zu\n", sizeof(a), sizeof(c));
    printf("Seg: %llx %x\n", a, c);
    printf("Seg: %lx %x\n", a, c);
    printf("Seg: %x\n", c);
    return 0;
}

On a 64-bit machine, all works fine. On a 32-bit machine though, if I use an incorrect formatter for the first argument (second printf), I get incorrect output for second argument too. Is that because of how varargs are processed? What am I missing?

Output

Sizes: 8 4
Seg: 1111111122222222 33333333
Seg: 22222222 11111111
Seg: 33333333
a.out: ELF 32-bit LSB executable, Intel 80386, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked, interpreter /lib/ld-linux.so.2, for GNU/Linux 3.2.0, not stripped

Command used

rm ./a.out ; g++ -m32 test.cpp ; ./a.out ; file a.out
rows.key_body:
The second printf where the conversion format does not match the actual type passed has undefined behavior, so the C Standard imposes no requirements and anything you observe is possible, including expected behavior, as you observe on 64-bit targets and different behavior as you want to analyse on your 32-bit target.

Here is a tentative explanation (assuming little endian and stack based ABI):

  • on your 32-bit target, vararg arguments are passed on the stack, 32-bit aligned
  • passing an unsigned long long uses 2 stack slots in little endian order
  • passing an unsigned int uses a single slot
  • on this target, unsigned long, expected by printf for %lx has 32 bits (as is the case on most targets), so it uses a single slot
  • hence in this target, the first number is retrieved from the first slot and the value is the low 32-bits of the 64-bit value passed in little endian order
  • the second number is retrieved from the second slot, where the most significant 32-bits have been stored by the caller.
  • this explains the output: Seg: 22222222 11111111

Remember that undefined behavior is by definition not defined, so other side effects may happen and something completely different may be output, even on the same host with the same binary.

As commented by @GlennWillen, in particular, you cannot count on the damage being limited to a particular line of code, or function, or file; and you cannot count on it being limited to consequences which would actually be possible in any straightforward interpretation of the code; and you cannot count on it being limited to things happening chronologically after the UB in many cases. If the code could execute UB when some condition is true, the compiler may act as though that condition is false everywhere and for all purposes, even if this is absurd or contradictory.

Here are some take-aways:

  • always turn on extra warnings so this kind of bug is reported by the compiler (-Wall -Wextra or similar).
  • fix the code to compile without any warnings (adding -Werror will force this) and think twice before using casts to silence a warning.
  • use the formatting macros from <inttypes.h> for types defined in <stdint.h>
rows.title: Why does a mismatching printf specifier also affect subsequent arguments?

rows.body:
Two programs below differ only in how they mention &inited_with_side_effect<> in the default template argument of template variable v. In both, I expect inited_with_side_effect<0> is instantiated and its dynamic initializer prints INIT.

Is the instantiation/print required, or may an implementation omit it? Compilers disagree, and they disagree on different programs.

A. Address encoded in a type

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>

template <int = 0>
char inited_with_side_effect = (std::puts("INIT"), 0);

template <typename = std::integral_constant<char *, &inited_with_side_effect<>>>
constexpr int v = 0;

int main() {
    return v<>;
}

B. Address as an auto NTTP

#include <cstdio>

template <int = 0>
char inited_with_side_effect = (std::puts("INIT"), 0);

template <auto = &inited_with_side_effect<>>
constexpr int v = 0;

int main() {
    return v<>;
}

Observed (INIT printed or not)

A (typename = integral_constant<…>) B (auto = &…)
GCC no print prints INIT
Clang prints INIT prints INIT
MSVC prints INIT no print

So far: GCC omits the print on A; MSVC omits it on B.

Compiler Explorer: https://godbolt.org/z/ff6daY3nb

Why it might have to print

The expression &inited_with_side_effect<> in the default template argument is potentially evaluated if you take the definition in [basic.def.odr] literally.

The default template argument is also "instantiated" because it is needed by return v<>; ([temp.arg.general]).

[basic.def.odr]: a variable named by a potentially evaluated expression is odr-used unless an exception applies. Unary & does not apply lvalue-to-rvalue conversion, and this object is a non-const non-constexpr char, so it is not usable in constant expressions. Taking its address looks like an odr-use.

[temp.inst]: a variable template specialization is implicitly instantiated when it is referenced in a context that requires a variable definition to exist. Odr-use is the usual such context.

If that specialization is instantiated, it is a non-block non-inline variable with static storage duration.

[basic.start.dynamic]: It is implementation-defined whether the dynamic initialization of a non-block non-inline variable with static storage duration is sequenced before the first statement of main or is deferred. If it is deferred, it strongly happens before any non-initialization odr-use of any non-inline function or non-inline variable defined in the same translation unit as the variable to be initialized.

main is a non-inline function defined in the same TU and calling it is a non-initialization odr-use. So initialization of inited_with_side_effect<0>, deferred or not, should strongly happen before main's first statement. The same chapter also says that a non-local static-storage variable whose initialization has side effects is initialized in this situation even if that variable is not itself odr-used.

Questions

  1. Are these compiler bugs? Or does any rule in the standard permit skipping the definition / the dynamic initializer?

  2. If v<...> is never used, should the side effect still happen?
rows.key_body:
Instantiation of default template arguments is underspecified (see CWG1635) but the OP's examples, surprisingly, fall within the bounds of what very little the standard does say clearly. See [temp.arg.general]/10:

When a simple-template-id or splice-specialization-specifier does not designate a function, a default template-argument is implicitly instantiated when the value of that default argument is needed.
[Example 7:

template<typename T, typename U = int>
struct S { };
S<bool>* p;         // the type of p is S<bool, int>*

The default argument for U is instantiated to form the type S<bool, int>*. — end example]

It's clear: merely mentioning the simple-template-id v<> is enough to force instantiation of its default argument. Then, as you say, since the expression &inited_with_side_effect<> is potentially evaluated, it constitutes an odr-use of that variable and forces its instantiation.

A more interesting question is whether inited_with_side_effect<> should still be instantiated if v<> isn't mentioned in the program. The standard doesn't give a clear answer to that.
rows.title: Must a variable template be instantiated when it appears only as `&x` in a default template argument?

rows.body:
I have a hash table with the key type std::array<uint8_t,6>, and I am trying to come up with as fast hash function as possible. One option is to pack all six 8-bit integers into a single 64-bit integer first, and then just use std::hash<uint64_t>. I've tried two different ways how to resolve this packing, one based on casting and shifting, the second one based on memcpy.

uint64_t pack(std::array<uint8_t, 6> key) {
  return
    (static_cast<uint64_t>(key[0]) << 0) 
      | (static_cast<uint64_t>(key[1]) << 8) 
      | (static_cast<uint64_t>(key[2]) << 16) 
      | (static_cast<uint64_t>(key[3]) << 24) 
      | (static_cast<uint64_t>(key[4]) << 32) 
      | (static_cast<uint64_t>(key[5]) << 40);
}

uint64_t pack(std::array<uint8_t, 6> key) {
  uint64_t tmp{};
  std::memcpy(&tmp, key.data(), 6);
  return tmp;
}

In both these cases, I got an optimal machine code with Clang, where key (passed by register) is only masked. However, GCC produced much less optimized machine code with many more instructions. I primarily use GCC in practice, so I would like to get the optimized machine code with GCC as well; any help would be appreciated.

Online demo: https://godbolt.org/z/zebxMxdq8

(For completeness, there is also an option to use the array hasher from Boost.)
rows.title: GCC vs Clang when packing array<uint8_t,N> into uint64_t

rows.body:
Is there a way to declare an enumeration that has multiple representations, for example a numeric and a string?

The intent here is to create an enum class with multiple values, each of which has 2 different representations, a numeric and a string. Either representation is valid and unique across the enumeration.

A private constructor is included to prevent the addition of new enumerated values.

The attributes numericCode and alphaCode represent the 2 representations of the enum.

    enum class Foo {
        Value01 { 001, "aa" },
        Value02 { 002, "bb" },
         .....
        ValueN. { nn, "zz" };
    private:
        Foo( int numeric, const string alpha ) : numericCode( numeric ), alphaCode( alpha ) {}
    private:
        int    numericCode;
        string alphaCode;
    };

Rationale for this is to avoid a common construct of performing string or numeric comparisons for when determining an enumerated case; avoid multiple symbols for magic numbers across situationally convenient compilation units, or hard to maintain hard coded magic numbers throughout the codebase, etc.

ISO 3166 is a real world example of this. There are multiple codes that represent a country; a 2-character alpha, a 3-character alpha, and a 3-digit number. Each code uniquely represents a specific enumerated value, while multiple representations may uniquely identify a single enumerated value.

This is the goal, but in Java:

public enum Foo {
    Value01 ( 001, "aa" ),
    Value02 ( 002, "bb" ),
    ValueNN ( 999, "zz" );

    private final int    numericCode;
    private final String alphaCode;

    Foo( final int numeric, final String alpha ) {
        numericCode = numeric;
        alphaCode   = alpha;
    }

    public String getAlpha() {
        return alphaCode;
    }

    public int getNumeric() {
        return numericCode;
    }
}

I attempted the pseudo code in the question. I have implemented this in Java a number of times.
rows.key_body:
The thing you want to achieve does not work with enums in C++. An enum in C++ is just an integer, which has symbolic names for the different values it can take.

You can create something that behaves essentially the same as Java's enum like this:

// Put this is a header file
struct FooValue_ {
  int numeric;
  const char* text;
private:
  constexpr FooValue_(int n, const char* s) : numeric(n), text(s) {}
  FooValue_(const FooValue_&) = delete;
  friend class Foo;
};

class Foo {
public:
  typedef const FooValue_* Value;
private:
  static const constexpr FooValue_ Value1_{1, "aa"};
  static const constexpr FooValue_ Value2_{2, "bb"};
public:
  static const constexpr Value Value1 = &Value1_;
  static const constexpr Value Value2 = &Value2_;
};

// put this in a source file (and include the header file)
#include <ostream>   // operator<< for std::ostream
#include <iostream>  // std::cout

int main(void)
{
  Foo::Value v1 = Foo::Value1;
  Foo::Value v2 = Foo::Value2;
  std::cout << v1->numeric << ' ' << v2->text << '\n';

  // switch via unique numeric member
  switch (v1->numeric)
  {
    case Foo::Value1->numeric:
      std::cout << "Is Value1\n";
      break;
    case Foo::Value2->numeric:
      std::cout << "Is Value2\n";
      break;
  }

  // if/else via identity (this is likely what happens with Java enums)
  if (v2 == Foo::Value1) {
      std::cout << "Is Value1\n";
  } else if (v2 == Foo::Value2) {
      std::cout << "Is Value2\n";
  }
}

The idea is to have the numeric and the text value grouped in a struct (the type called FooValue_), and limit the creation of instances of that struct to one specific region, namely the class Foo itself. I do this by making the constructor of FooValue_ private and making the class Foo a friend. That's also the reason why Foo needs to be a class instead of a namespace, even though no instances of foo are ever created (you might want to add a deleted constructor to Foo).

To use this "fake Java Enum", you use the address of the instances created inside the Foo class as pointer values. To hide the gory details from the user, a typedef Foo::Value is provided, and the enumerators that are exposed to the user are not the structures themselves, but pointers to them. You still see the pointer-ness of this approach by the need to use -> instead of . to access the members.

While you can't switch on this kind of "fake Java enum", you can switch either on the numeric value, or use an if/else chain, as shown in the code snippet.
rows.title: Is there a way in C++ to have a scoped enum containing multiple representations?

In C++, there are some widely used zero-size base classes used for the purpose of "tagging" subclasses, for example boost::noncopyable.

Is there any that is used to mark a class non-instantiable, like a "static class" in C#?

Before you tell me I should be using a namespace for this: my class has template arguments, namespaces can't.

If there's no accepted "tag", is there a pattern that a compiler can use to recognize the static class pattern and generate warnings if a non-static member is accidentally created?

template<typename my_trait>
struct X
{
   ~X() = delete;

   static int N; // I don't need this but static data members are typically allowed for static classes
   int x; // warning please!
   static bool f(typename my_trait::f_arg arg); // ok
   bool g(); // warning please!
};
rows.key_body:
Whilst namespaces can't have template arguments, things declared in namespaces can.

namespace X
{
template<typename my_trait>
int N;

template<typename my_trait>
bool f(typename my_trait::f_arg arg);
}

Yes this means that uses of this will be X::N<foo> and X::f<foo>(bar) instead of X<foo>::N and X<foo>::f(bar). You will also be repeating template<typename my_trait> a whole lot.

rows.body:
The problem started appearing after upgrading from Java 21 to 25.

With Java 21, my menus looked like this :

With Java 25, a gutter started appearing :

I've created minimal portable example to reproduce :

import java.awt.Color;
import java.awt.Graphics2D;
import java.awt.event.ActionEvent;
import java.awt.event.ActionListener;
import java.awt.image.BufferedImage;

import javax.swing.AbstractAction;
import javax.swing.Action;
import javax.swing.ButtonGroup;
import javax.swing.ImageIcon;
import javax.swing.JCheckBoxMenuItem;
import javax.swing.JFrame;
import javax.swing.JMenu;
import javax.swing.JMenuBar;
import javax.swing.JMenuItem;
import javax.swing.JRadioButtonMenuItem;
import javax.swing.SwingUtilities;
import javax.swing.UIManager;
import javax.swing.WindowConstants;

public class IconMenuExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        // we set the Windows Look And Feel
        UIManager.setLookAndFeel("com.sun.java.swing.plaf.windows.WindowsLookAndFeel");

        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> {

            JFrame frame = new JFrame("Menu Icon Example");

            JMenuBar menuBar = new JMenuBar();
            JMenu fileMenu = new JMenu("File");

            // we create sample actions using programmatic sixteen by sixteen ImageIcon instances
            Action openAction = newAction(
                    "Open",
                    createColorIcon(Color.BLUE),
                    e -> System.out.println("Open")
            );

            Action saveAction = newAction(
                    "Save",
                    createColorIcon(Color.GREEN),
                    e -> System.out.println("Save")
            );

            Action exitAction = newAction(
                    "Exit",
                    createColorIcon(Color.RED),
                    e -> System.exit(0)
            );

            // we attach the actions to menu items
            fileMenu.add(new JMenuItem(openAction));
            fileMenu.add(new JMenuItem(saveAction));
            fileMenu.addSeparator();
            fileMenu.add(new JMenuItem(exitAction));

            // we create the second menu with check box menu items
            JMenu optionsMenu = new JMenu("Options");

            JCheckBoxMenuItem checkOne = new JCheckBoxMenuItem("Enable Feature One");
            checkOne.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("Feature One toggled: " + checkOne.isSelected()));

            JCheckBoxMenuItem checkTwo = new JCheckBoxMenuItem("Enable Feature Two");
            checkTwo.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("Feature Two toggled: " + checkTwo.isSelected()));

            optionsMenu.add(checkOne);
            optionsMenu.add(checkTwo);

            // we create the third menu with radio button menu items
            JMenu modeMenu = new JMenu("Mode");

            JRadioButtonMenuItem modeA = new JRadioButtonMenuItem("Mode A");
            JRadioButtonMenuItem modeB = new JRadioButtonMenuItem("Mode B");
            JRadioButtonMenuItem modeC = new JRadioButtonMenuItem("Mode C");

            ButtonGroup modeGroup = new ButtonGroup();
            modeGroup.add(modeA);
            modeGroup.add(modeB);
            modeGroup.add(modeC);

            modeA.setSelected(true);

            modeA.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("Mode A selected"));
            modeB.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("Mode B selected"));
            modeC.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("Mode C selected"));

            modeMenu.add(modeA);
            modeMenu.add(modeB);
            modeMenu.add(modeC);

            // we add all menus to the bar
            menuBar.add(fileMenu);
            menuBar.add(optionsMenu);
            menuBar.add(modeMenu);

            frame.setJMenuBar(menuBar);

            frame.setSize(300, 200);
            frame.setLocationRelativeTo(null);
            frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(WindowConstants.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
            frame.setVisible(true);
        });
    }

    public static Action newAction(String name, ImageIcon icon, ActionListener listener) {
        Action action = new AbstractAction(name) {
            @Override
            public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
                listener.actionPerformed(e);
            }
        };
        action.putValue(Action.SMALL_ICON, icon);
        return action;
    }

    // we create a programmatic sixteen by sixteen ImageIcon filled with the given color
    private static ImageIcon createColorIcon(Color color) {
        int size = 16;
        BufferedImage image = new BufferedImage(size, size, BufferedImage.TYPE_INT_ARGB);
        Graphics2D g = image.createGraphics();
        try {
            g.setColor(color);
            g.fillRect(0, 0, size, size);
        } finally {
            g.dispose();
        }
        return new ImageIcon(image);
    }
}

It's a reserved space for checkboxes and radio buttons as 2nd and 3rd menu illustrate. However, when there's none, it would make sense not to show that gutter.

    callq    exit
                                        # -- End function
    .addrsig

Since compilers don't really do this, I think I might be wrong, but I don't understand why I'm wrong, and I want to know if I'm correct.
rows.key_body:
One major reason for not looking for your proposed optimization is that it's super niche (noreturn functions are rare), and doesn't save instructions. Also, it would conflict with keeping any of your own local vars in your incoming shadow space, and many functions have local vars.

(Compiler devs have to balance the value of an optimization against the amount of compile time it takes to look for it, and the maintenance / testing burden of the compiler code that looks for it. Not just the development time of a new feature, but ongoing cost in slower builds, larger source code, and something that could potentially break and lead to miscompiled programs when other parts of the compiler internals are being reworked.)

It only helps with speed by reusing a cache line of stack space that's already hot... once in the lifetime of a thread. Sure you could construct a corner case where this avoids a page fault to grow the stack, but very often the saving would be totally trivial.

Often a tailcall is possible (like jmp exit) and does as good a job at giving our shadow space to a callee. (exit may be marked as special to have GCC not tailcall it, so debuggers can see where it was called from. abort() is marked that way, so the backtrace it generates doesn't omit its actual caller. Or maybe your GCC just chooses to use call instead of add $40, %rsp / jmp exit since it already has the stack set up for a call. And that's fine since the stack memory below RSP is probably already hot in cache since we just make another call.)

As far as I can tell, GCC doesn't seem to have any special attributes other than noreturn for functions like abort: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Common-Function-Attributes.html#index-noreturn-function-attribute says - In order to preserve backtraces, GCC will never turn calls to noreturn functions into tail calls. So doing other things that break backtraces should also be avoided for callers of noreturn functions. This proposed optimization would still allow seeing which function called abort, but not further up the call stack: what you're doing is almost like a tailcall, but we overwrite our incoming return address with a return address into this function. So instead of skipping ourselves in the call-chain, we break the chain, losing any reference to our parent function.
(Semi-related: Why does the C compiler save registers in a noreturn function?)

Allocating local variables (other than incoming register args) into shadow space is something MSVC does (but not GCC or Clang), since that's a generally useful optimization and it can save instructions in leaf functions, or ones that exit via tailcall, if they never have to move RSP at all.
(Godbolt - MSVC does it for volatile int a,b;, volatile long long a,b (16 bytes), or volatile int arr[2], but not for volatile int arr[4]; (16 bytes))

e.g. void foo(){ volatile long long a=1; } compiles with MSVC to mov QWORD PTR a$[rsp], 1 / ret, where a$ is defined as a$ = 8 in its asm listing. So this is the first slot of shadow space.

Saving stack space isn't totally irrelevant; the same compilers we use for user-space are also used to compile kernel code. Kernel stacks are often 8K or 16K per thread, and not pageable. (Linux used to use 4K kernel stacks on 32-bit x86, but last I checked had raised it again for x86-64 from 8 to 16K. I don't know what Windows does.)

So it's good if compilers don't waste stack space gratuitously, but even 48 bytes is not much out of 8K if it only happens a couple times in a call chain. And noreturn functions are vanishingly rare in kernel code, especially higher up in the callstack where the space would be wasted across calls to many callees. (In kernel code, everything except ending a thread/task will return to user-space.) So this is probably irrelevant there. And as @chqrlie says, stack space is not a precious commodity in user-space on x86-64. Windows by default uses 1MiB user-space stacks, GNU/Linux 8MiB.

Most calling-conventions that GCC targets don't have shadows space, only a few like MIPS and Windows x64, so I'm not surprised it doesn't have optimization passes to look for ways to get the best use out of it. x86-64 is the most important target for MSVC, so it's a good thing it does better at using it for locals.
rows.title: Why doesn't the Windows C compiler reuse incoming shadow space in noreturn functions?

rows.key_body:
std::format insists that its format string argument should be a compile time constant.

I thought this was so that std::format could be used to create compile time constant values.

It is not. The motivation for std::format's format string to be a constant is to allow compile-time type checking of the format string. So that something like std::format("x={}") is a compile error, rather than a runtime error.

Is there a solution, or a workaround, to this? Or am I simply missing something which can make this work.

std::format itself is not constexpr (yet). There is no workaround.

Note also that you can still provide non-constant format strings to std::format, you just have to wrap the format string in std::runtime_format:

int main()
{
    std::print("Hello {}!\n", "world");
 
    std::string fmt;
    for (int i{}; i != 3; ++i)
    {
        fmt += "{} "; // constructs the formatting string
        std::print("{} : ", fmt);
        std::println(std::runtime_format(fmt), "alpha", 'Z', 3.14, "unused");
    }
}
rows.title: Using std::format to create compile time objects with constexpr

rows.key_body:
Three things come to mind:

1. Deduction

When invoking (overloaded) template functions, template argument deduction will deduce the free types. Presumably, you're already aware of this part (because you are using variadics in your example).

c++17 CTAD extends this to constructors of types, e.g. std::vector { 1,2,3 } becomes std::vector<int, std::allocator<int> >, std::array { 1,2,3 } becomes std::array<int, 3>.

2. Template Aliases:

You can either use template aliases:

template <typename K, typename V, typename Pair = std::pair<K const, V> >
using MyMap = boost::container::flat_map<K, V, std::less<K>, 
                      boost::container::small_vector<Pair, 10> >;

Now you can use the unwieldy type name as

MyMap<std::string, double> m;

3. Opaque types / Concepts

In reality, you don't usually care about all the subsidiary details. For example, you might only require a "Range", or a "Container" or a "Map", not some specific instance.

Instead of

template <typename TA, size_t NA> struct Address {
    std::array<TA, NA> details;
};
template <typename TO, size_t NO> struct Owner {
    std::array<TO, NO> details;
};
template <typename... Ts> struct HouseRoomsLayout {
    std::tuple<Ts...> data_;
};
template <typename TA, size_t NA, typename TO, size_t NO, typename... Ts> struct House {
    Address<TA, NA>         address_;
    Owner<TO, NO>           owner_;
    HouseRoomsLayout<Ts...> layout_;
};

You could write

template <typename TA, size_t NA> struct Address {
    std::array<TA, NA> details;
};
template <typename TO, size_t NO> struct Owner {
    std::array<TO, NO> details;
};
template <typename... Ts> struct HouseRoomsLayout {
    std::tuple<Ts...> data_;
    HouseRoomsLayout(Ts const&... room) : data_(room...) {}
};

template <class T, class... U> Address(T, U...) -> Address<T, 1 + sizeof...(U)>;
template <class T, class... U> Owner(T, U...) -> Owner<T, 1 + sizeof...(U)>;

template <typename Address, typename Owner, typename Layout> struct House {
    Address address_;
    Owner   owner_;
    Layout  layout_;
};

auto create_house_from(auto address, auto owner, auto... rooms) {
    std::cout << __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ << std::endl;
    return House{address, owner, HouseRoomsLayout{std::move(rooms)...}};
}

int main() {
    Address addr{"Hello Inc"s, "World Drive 42", "Cincinatti", "Uganda"};
    Owner   owner{999}; // imagining an ID type here

    struct Room { std::vector<int> furniture; } backroom;
    struct Garage { std::vector<int> tools; } garage;
    HouseRoomsLayout layout{ backroom, garage };

    auto h = create_house_from(addr, owner, layout);

    return 0;
}

Better yet, you wouldn't need create_XXX_from anymore, since that's what CTAD was invented for:

    auto h = House{addr, owner, layout};

creates the exact same house. In fact, go ham!

Live On Coliru

#include <array>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>
using namespace std::string_literals;

template <typename TA, size_t NA> struct Address { std::array<TA, NA> details; };
template <typename TO, size_t NO> struct Owner   { std::array<TO, NO> details; };
template <typename... Ts> struct HouseRoomsLayout {
    std::tuple<Ts...> data_;
    HouseRoomsLayout(Ts const&... room) : data_(room...) {}
};

template <class T, class... U> Address(T, U...) -> Address<T, 1 + sizeof...(U)>;
template <class T, class... U> Owner(T, U...) -> Owner<T, 1 + sizeof...(U)>;

template <typename Address, typename Owner, typename Layout> struct House {
    Address address_;
    Owner   owner_;
    Layout  layout_;
};

int main() {
    struct Room   { std::vector<int> furniture; } backroom;
    struct Garage { std::vector<int> tools;     } garage;

    auto h = House{
        Address{"Hello Inc"s, "World Drive 42", "Cincinatti", "Uganda"},
        Owner{999},
        HouseRoomsLayout{backroom, garage},
    };
}

Caveat

I'm assuming you're learning about things here. The presented design does not seem like good interface design. At the very least, if you need all that flexibility, make concepts for the different classes of types.

rows.body:
I'm trying to persist the last modification timestamp of a set of files in a Git repository. I understand that Git doesn't natively support tracking filesystem metadata, so some sort of customization is due.

For purposes of illustration, consider the following repository structure:

/
├─ meta.inf
├─+ doc
│ └─ notes.md
└─+ data
  ├─ 1.csv
  └─ 2.csv

Here is what I'm trying to accomplish: Before changes to the repository are to be materialized,

  • if any file under the data directory was modified, then
    • find the most recent filesystem modification timestamp among those modified files, and
    • write that timestamp to meta.inf.

How can this be done?

Since this is inevitably going to require some amount of scripting (and setup), I'm looking for a solution that works on Windows, using batch and/or PowerShell as the scripting environment.

Relaxing constraints

Commenters alerted me to the fact that storing concepts (like filesystem metadata) in a Git repository that Git doesn't natively understand can lead to conflicts that cannot be unambiguously resolved. To that end, I am fine with a solution that assumes a single source of changes.

Non-solutions

This came up in comments, more than once, so I want to clarify that I'm not looking for solutions that suggest using a Git commit object's timestamp as a proxy. While this may work "for most people", it isn't suitable for my use case. The closely related Checking out old files WITH original create/modified timestamps fails the "works on Windows" requirement. There's a lot of useful information over there that can be used to inspire a solution, but it doesn't directly answer my question.
rows.key_body:
Since you're looking for an event-based solution (updating a metadata file on commit), a client-side Git hook is needed, specifically a pre-commit hook.

Note that Git on Windows comes with its own Bash shell and common Unix utilities, so a cross-platform solution is possible.

However, the following proof-of-concept for Windows delegates the work to Windows PowerShell, via its powershell.exe CLI.

  • It would even be easy to adapt the solution to Unix-like platforms (as an alternative to a pure Bash solution), given the availability of PowerShell (Core) 7, the modern, cross-platform, install-on-demand edition: all it takes is to replace powershell.exe with pwsh in the code below.

  • Note that it is possible to make hook scripts run PowerShell code directly (rather than having to call the PowerShell CLI from a /bin/sh-interpreted script), though it requires a workaround: see the bottom section.

  • Either way, on Windows the assumption is that execution of PowerShell scripts has already been allowed on a given target machine (on Unix-like platforms this isn't necessary), such as with one-time configuration command
    Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned -Force; if not, you can enable script execution ad hoc by adding -ExecutionPolicy Bypass to the CLI calls, assuming that there aren't more restrictive GPO-based policies in place; see this answer for more information.

  • To also address the aspect of avoiding potential merge conflicts caused by meta.inf involving multiple repository clones, see VonC's helpful answer.

Setting up the pre-commmit hook:

  • From your repo's root directory, create file ./git/hooks/pre-commit, e.g., from PowerShell, with
    New-Item ./git/hooks/pre-commit

    • Note: On Unix-like platforms you'd need to make this file executable, using
      chmod +x ./git/hooks/pre-commit, but this isn't needed on Windows (where you'd have to invoke the command from Git Bash if you were to invoke it; however, on Windows all files default to having the executable (x) permission from Git Bash's perspective).

  • Place the following content in the file:

#!/bin/sh

# Among the files to be committed that reside in data/,
# determine the most recent last-modified timestamp
# and write it to 'meta.inf' and make the modified 'meta.inf' part of the commit.
powershell.exe -noprofile -c '
  git diff --cached --name-only data/ |
    Get-Item -Force -ErrorAction Ignore |
    Sort-Object -Property LastWriteTime |
    Select-Object -Last 1 |
    ForEach-Object {
      "[data]", "MostRecentLastModified=$($_.LastWriteTime.ToString("o"))" |
        Set-Content -ErrorAction Stop meta.inf
      git add meta.inf
      exit $LASTEXITCODE
    }
  exit 0
'

Note:

  • git diff --cached --name-only data/ ensures that only files in the data/ subdirectory tree that are part of the ongoing commit are processed.

  • The above assumes that meta.inf is expected to conform to the Inf file format, using the self-chosen names [data] for the section and MostRecentLastModified for the key; adjust as needed.

  • The timestamp is using .NET's round-trip date-time string format; e.g.
    2025-12-04T11:38:15.8774146-05:00

  • Example meta.inf content:

    [data]
MostRecentLastModified=2025-12-04T11:38:15.8774146-05:00
Alternative: Making Git hook scripts "speak" PowerShell directly:

  • As discussed, the above uses a PowerShell CLI call from a /bin/sh-interpreted script, using the -c (-Command) parameter to pass the PowerShell code as an argument.

    • Doing so comes with quoting challenges, because embedding ' chars. to pass through to PowerShell inside a Bash '...' string is awkward ('\'')

    • Sadly, providing the code via stdin (which would allow using a verbatim Bash here-document) is not an option, because PowerShell exhibits unexpected pseudo-interactive behavior in this case; see GitHub issue #3223.

  • Sadly, directly using a shebang line that targets PowerShell (e.g. #!/usr/bin/env powershell (WinPS) or #!/usr/bin/env pwsh), does not work, for the reasons detailed in this answer. However, the linked answer also demonstrates a workaround, which is applied below; for cross-platform and/or PowerShell (Core) 7 use, replace powershell with pwsh in the 2nd line of code.

    • If you'd like see direct support for PowerShell shebang lines in a future PS7 version (some version post-v7.5.x), you can signal your interest by giving GitHub issue #26584 a 👍.
#!/bin/sh
tmpPs1Script="$(mktemp --suffix=.ps1)"; tail +3 "$0" > "$tmpPs1Script"; powershell -NoProfile -File "$tmpPs1Script"; ec=$?; rm "$tmpPs1Script"; exit $ec

# The two lines above in effect cause the rest of this file 
# to be interpreted by PowerShell.

git diff --cached --name-only data/ |
  Get-Item -Force -ErrorAction Ignore |
  Sort-Object -Property LastWriteTime |
  Select-Object -Last 1 |
  ForEach-Object {
    "[data]", "MostRecentLastModified=$($_.LastWriteTime.ToString("o"))" |
      Set-Content -ErrorAction Stop meta.inf
    git add meta.inf
    exit $LASTEXITCODE
  }

exit 0
rows.title: Retain the exact modification timestamp of a file in a Git repository

My code reliably finds a precise (similar value every time) but in the region of 3.24 and 3.26. Competent mathematicians will note this around 0.1 away from an ideal Pi value.

My code revolves around picking random points on a 10,000 x 10,000 grid. The hypotenuse with respect to (0,0) is calculated and if this hypotenuse is less than 10,000, the point is inside a theoretical circle with radius 10,000.

The ratio of points inside and all points multiplied by 4 should give an estimation for Pi.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <math.h>
#include <time.h>

int RandomNum(int min, int max);

int main()
{
    int d = 0;
    int n = 0;
    srand(time(NULL));


    for (int i =0; i < 10000; i++)
    {
        n++;
        int xI = RandomNum(-10000, 10000);
        //double xF = (double) xI/10000;
        printf("\nx: %f", xI);

        int yI = RandomNum(-10000, 10000);
        //double yF = (double) yI/10000;
        printf("\ny: %f", yI);

        double pythag = sqrt(xI*xI+yI*yI);
        printf("\nhyp: %f\n\n",pythag);

        if (pythag < 10000)
        {
            d++;
        }

    }
    printf("d = %d\n", d);
    printf("n = %d\n", n);
    double DNratio = (double) d/n;
    double PiEstimate = DNratio * 4;
    printf("Pi Estimate: %f", PiEstimate);
    return 0;
}
int RandomNum(int min, int max)
{
  int r = rand()%(max - min + 1) + min;
  return r;
}

//https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/c/generating-random-number-range-c/
//https://www.tutorialspoint.com/c_standard_library/c_function_srand.htm
rows.key_body:
The behavior you're seeing is most likely the result of a modulo bias, due to the small RAND_MAX value that is being used by the specific C library/compiler's implementation of the rand() function.

I get similar results to yours when testing with MSVC (x86 msvc v19.latest), where the RAND_MAX value is just 32,767. Using a modulo 10,000 operation (% 10000) on the output of rand() will generate "random" numbers with a very significant bias towards the lower numbers.(1) This causes more points to fall within your circle than you would normally expect, and results in an inflated estimated value of π.(2)

To demonstrate this: if we pick the random values between 0 and 32,767 and compare the hypotenuse with that value, we eliminate the modulo bias altogether, and the results much more closely approach the value of π as can be seen here:(3)

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <math.h>
#include <time.h>

int main()
{
    int d = 0;
    int n = 0;
    srand(time(NULL));

    for (int i =0; i < 10000; i++)
    {
        n++;
        int xI = rand();
        int yI = rand();

        double pythag = sqrt(xI*xI + yI*yI);

        if (pythag <= RAND_MAX)
        {
            d++;
        }
    }
    
    printf("d = %d\n", d);
    printf("n = %d\n", n);
    double DNratio = ((double) d)/n;
    double PiEstimate = DNratio * 4;
    printf("Pi Estimate: %f", PiEstimate); // yields ≈3.14
    return 0;
}

(1) Your implementation actually seems to be doing modulo 20,001, resulting in an even bigger bias. For a RAND_MAX value of 32,767, the rand() % 20001 operation produces numbers in the interval [0 .. 12,766] twice as often as numbers in the interval [12,767 .. 20,000].
(2) When using a compiler with a larger RAND_MAX value (like x86_64 gcc (trunk) where it's 2,147,483,647), the bias is much less noticeable, but still there.
(3) This of course doesn't negate the effects of the relatively small random sample size, and the inherent bias of the PRNG itself.
rows.title: Estimation for Pi is precise but inaccurate

I tried to write the following code and it was rejected by the compiler:

#include <type_traits>
struct Base {
    virtual void f() {}
};

template <typename T>
struct Derived : Base {
    virtual void f() requires std::is_same_v<T, int> override {}
};

I found the relevant section in the standard here:

11.7.3 Virtual functions
6 A virtual function shall not have a trailing requires-clause ([dcl.decl]).
[Example 5:

template<typename T>
struct A {
   virtual void f() requires true;       // error: virtual function cannot be constrained ([temp.constr.decl])
};

— end example]

but I don't understand the motivation behind this. Seeing as it is perfectly reasonable for a derived class not to override a base class' virtual function, why is it not considered OK to decide whether this override exists based on a (compile time) constraint?

This restriction seems particularly silly (at least in this example), since this code is legal and achieves essentially the same thing more verbosely:

template <typename T>
struct Derived : Base {
};

template <typename T>
requires std::is_same_v<T, int>
struct Derived<T> : Base {
    virtual void f() override {}
};

Edit

I seem to have caused some confusion by my omission of the virtual specifiers on the override functions in Derived. I have added them to make it clear that I'm intending to override the base class' virtual function (with another virtual function).
rows.key_body:
Why?

Because the standard says so :)

I would say that the rationale is to avoid having to decide whether different requires hide or override base function.

Imagine valid code:

template <int I>
concept isEven = ((I % 2) == 0);

template <int I>
struct Base {

    void f() requires (isEven<I>) { std::cout << "even\n"; }
    void f() requires (isEven<I> && I == 0) { std::cout << "0\n"; }
    void f() requires (I == 1) { std::cout << "1\n"; }
};

Demo

Base<0> has actually 2 overloads f, one more specialized than the other (subsumption).

If you add virtual, would void f() override be allowed in the derived class? Should the override have the same requires clause as in the base class?

Forbidding it now allows to decide later whether it's required.
rows.title: Why doesn't C++ allow virtual function overrides to be constrained by a concept/requires clause?

I've been using _aligned_malloc(), so far and realized that C++ has an aligned new operator since C++17.

I've read this StackOverflow question regarding the use of aligned new; the accepted answer there suggests usage as in the following example:

#include <new>

int* allocate() {
    return new (std::align_val_t(16)) int[40]; // 128-bit alignment
    // will call `void* operator new[](size_t, align_val_t)`
}

but when I try this with MSVC, I get error C2956.

To put it simply, what is C++17 aligned new (new operator by providing alignment), not something like std::aligned_alloc, equivalent for the following:

unsigned char* p = static_cast<unsigned char*>(_aligned_malloc(256, 64));
_aligned_free(static_cast<void*>(p));

using aligned new?

Exactly equivalent code example will be appreciated.

I've tried

unsigned char* p = new (std::align_val_t{64}) unsigned char[256];

but it also emitted throws error C2956. I think there will be built-in expression similar to previous code likely exists.

unsigned char* p = static_cast<unsigned char*>(::operator new(256, std::align_val_t{64}));
::operator delete(p, std::align_val_t{64});

works. But I am not sure it is equivalent to _aligned_malloc/_aligned_free code.
rows.key_body:
The first thing to remember is that Microsoft Visual C++ compiler is rather flakey, and cannot be fully trusted for proper standards compliance. Indeed, if we compile (GodBolt.org) the same code snippet with clang or with gcc, it works.

You can, instead, write the following:

int* allocate() {
    return static_cast<int*>(operator new[] (40 * sizeof(int),
                                             std::align_val_t(16)));
}

and this proper C++17 code, so it should work with all compliant compilers.

Don't forget: After allocating this way, you must deallocate with the corresponding delete[] operator, not just any delete! It will have to be

operator delete[](ptr, std::align_val_t(16));

PS - If you want to avoid the new mess, you should in principle be able to just invoke std::aligned_alloc(), also introduced with C++17... but, alas, MSVC refuses to accept that one as well for some reason.
rows.title: How can I use C++17 aligned new to replace _aligned_malloc?

Code

int main() {
    printf("hello");
    printf("hello");

}

Since I am not printing \n, I expected the terminal prompt to appear immediately after the output, on the same line, like this:

What actually happened: The output prints hellohello, but the prompt appears on the next line, as if a newline was added automatically:

PS C:\Users\Kannan\Desktop...> ./r.exe
hellohello

I know standard printf behavior does not flush a newline automatically. Is this behavior specific to the C runtime on Windows?

Raw output

PS C:\Users\Kannan\Desktop\K\L0\c++> gcc random_walk.c -o r
PS C:\Users\Kannan\Desktop\K\L0\c++> ./r.exe > output.txt
PS C:\Users\Kannan\Desktop\K\L0\c++> Format-Hex output.txt


           Path: C:\Users\Kannan\Desktop\K\L0\c++\output.txt

           00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F

00000000   FF FE 68 00 65 00 6C 00 6C 00 6F 00 68 00 65 00  .þh.e.l.l.o.h.e.
00000010   6C 00 6C 00 6F 00 0D 00 0A 00                    l.l.o.....

rows.key_body:
A since-deleted, putatively AI-generated answer (only users with sufficient reputation can view the link) actually provided good insights; let me provide a 100% human-generated perspective.

Your program works as intended; the behaviors you observe are specific to [Windows] PowerShell.

There are two distinct, unrelated aspects to consider:

  • (a) Printing external program output to the console (terminal).

  • (b) Capturing such output in a file, using >, i.e. I/O redirection.

Re (a)

By design, both cmd.exe and PowerShell - unlike most POSIX-compatible shells such as Bash[0] - ensure that a newline is always printed following command output before re-printing their prompt string in interactive sessions - even if the external program output does not end in a newline, such as in your case.

Thus, a program printing, say, printf("foo"); produces the same display output as one emitting printf("foo\n");:

Presumably, the design rationale is to ensure that the prompt string always prints at the start of a line, for visual consistency.
There is no way to modify this behavior in PowerShell that I am aware of.[1]

Re (b)

While it is understandable to try to use an I/O redirection, >, to capture an external program's raw byte output, this does not work as intended in Windows PowerShell, the legacy, ships-with-Windows, Windows-only edition of PowerShell whose latest and final version is 5.1:

  • External-program output is invariably first decoded, based on the encoding stored in [Console]::OutputEncoding, ...

  • ... and then re-encoded on saving to the target file, using the default encoding of the Out-File cmdlet, of which > is a virtual alias, and that default encoding happens to be UTF-16 LE (in which ASCII-range characters such as h are represented as 2-byte sequences with the low-order byte representing the ASCII code point and the high-order byte being 0x0, e.g. 68 00 for 'h'), preceded by a BOM (the FF FE by sequence shown at the start of your Format-Hex output).

  • Additionally, the external-program output is decoded line by line, and each line is written to the target file with a trailing newline, using the platform-native newline format, which is CRLF on Windows (\r\n, in printf terms) - whether or not the output's last line had a trailing newline.
    Thus, similarly to the to-console output, a program printing, say, printf("foo"); produces the same file content as one emitting printf("foo\n"); when redirected with >, the redirection operator

  • It is worth noting that even in PowerShell (Core) 7 (see below) the decoding behavior still applies with respect to further processing external-program output in memory, and the re-encoding behavior still applies when using explicit calls to file-saving cmdlets such as Out-File, though PowerShell 7 notably and commendably consistently defaults to BOM-less UTF-8.[2]

  • The simplest way to ensure capturing of raw bytes from external programs in Windows PowerShell is to delegate to cmd.exe, whose > operator does just that:

    # Windows PowerShell:
# Captures raw byte output from .\r.exe 
# Note: \ rather than / must be used for cmd.exe's sake.
cmd /c .\r.exe > output.txt

By contrast, it does work as intended in PowerShell (Core) 7, the modern, cross-platform, install-on-demand edition, in v7.4+ (older versions are now out of support), i.e. > captures raw byte output, the same way it does in cmd.exe and in POSIX-compatible shells such as Bash.

    # PowerShell (Core) 7.4+:
    # Captures raw byte output from ./r.exe, both on Windows and Unix-like platforms.
    ./r.exe > output.txt

[0] As Charlie Harding points out in a comment on the question, the lone exception among the major POSIX-compatible shells is zsh, which also ensures that a newline is printed, but additionally visually highlights the lack of a trailing newline in program output by following its last line with a % printed in reverse video; the - non-POSIX-compatible - fish shell uses ⏎ instead; see this blog post for details.

[1] By contrast, a hack is available if you use cmd.exe rather than PowerShell, as explained by Neil in a comment on the question: Batch files whose last line contains (just) : suppress the mechanism that implicitly adds a newline to the output from programs not ending in a newline, so you could wrap calls to such programs in such a batch file.

[2] Windows PowerShell is, unfortunately, wildly inconsistent with respect to default character encodings - see the bottom section of this answer.

rows.key_body:
The problem may not lie with fgets() and printf(). There are some problems with the way FIFO and socket operations are done

1. Change foo() in client.c to

void *foo(void *arg) {
    char buf[MAX_LINE];
    int fd = open("/tmp/myfifo", O_RDONLY);

    if (fd == -1) {
        perror("open");
        return NULL;
    }

    ssize_t n;
    while ((n = read(fd, buf, sizeof(buf))) > 0) {
        fwrite(buf, 1, n, stdout);
        fflush(stdout);
    }

    if (n < 0)
        perror("read");

    close(fd);
    return NULL;
}

This avoids repeatedly opening the FIFO, checks the number of bytes received, and prints exactly those bytes without assuming the buffer is null-terminated.

2. server.c replace it

write(fd, buf, sizeof(buf));

with

write(fd, buf, buf_len);

This prevents writing unused bytes from the buffer. For production code, also handle partial writes and errors.

3. Initialize addr_len before calling this fucntion accept()

addr_len = sizeof(sin);

4. Correct the socket receive loop -

while ((buf_len = recv(new_s, buf, sizeof(buf), 0)) > 0) {
    if (write(fd, buf, buf_len) == -1) {
        perror("write");
        break;
    }
}

if (buf_len < 0)
    perror("recv");

It is important to notice that the code provided does not account for negative values returned by recv(). In addition, the code needs to accommodate partial writes to FIFOs.

Notice: It is not required to reopen the FIFO on each read, although this might not be the root cause of the problem since the server has an open write descriptor for the FIFO.

These changes help to correct some errors in the provided program but do not explain the reason why the messages sent from the server are received only after hitting the Enter key because the client program already uses an additional thread to receive data.

As an alternative solution, one may consider either a separate thread for receiving messages via sockets or a select() call.

rows.body:
Any time you call document.createElement (or its cousins, e.g. createDocumentFragment), the new node belongs to that document. It's my understanding that if you add that new node to a different document, then it will be updated to belong to that other document, and everything will work fine.

I'm writing a factory function that creates elements given tag type, attributes, and children. I would rather not have to pass the document in as a parameter.

In a situation where there are multiple documents pertaining to an application (e.g. an iframe, or a child window), if all you're doing is creating new nodes and adding them to some document, is there any disadvantage to creating all of those nodes on the topmost document? E.g. are there any semantic differences, or performance costs?
rows.key_body:
For plain elements, honestly, nothing bad happens. I've built nodes in one document and dropped them into an iframe's document plenty of times, and the browser just adopts the node as you append it — its ownerDocument quietly switches over and everything works. I double-checked this in jsdom with two windows before answering: created a div in the top document, appended it into the iframe, ownerDocument flipped to the iframe's document, no error, text and all intact. There's no copying cost worth worrying about either, the node just gets re-parented.

Where it does bite is that a node never forgets which window created it. That same div, while living in the iframe, is instanceof the top window's HTMLDivElement and not the iframe's. So if any code in the target document (yours, or a library's) checks elements with instanceof against its own window's constructors, it'll say no to your imported nodes even though they're sitting right there in its tree.

Custom elements are the sharper edge. If I define x-foo in the iframe's window only, then topDocument.createElement('x-foo') gives me a plain un-upgraded element — the constructor doesn't run. It only upgrades once it actually lands in the iframe's document, so anything you configure between creating it and inserting it happens on an element that isn't your component yet.

So for a factory that only makes standard elements and inserts them straight away, I wouldn't bother threading the document through either. If custom elements or instanceof checks are anywhere in the picture, it's worth creating nodes in the document they'll live in — and you can get that document at insert time from the container itself, container.ownerDocument.createElement(...), without passing a document parameter around.
rows.title: Is there any disadvantage to calling document.createElement with the “wrong” document?

I'm creating a program to collect news items from the internet regarding companies, separate out the text from the html code and then allocate scoring depending on the information it contains. I've managed to create the program but it produced an error. I've pasted the full program at the bottom of this post but I think the error is happening in this code segment:

text = "".join(p.get_text(" ",strip=True)
    for p in paragraphs
    )

The full program is here:

import feedparser
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import sqlite3
import json

RSS_FEEDS = ["https://www.fool.co.uk/feed/",]

OLLAMA_MODEL = "llama3.1:7b"

conn=sqlite3.connect('investment_news.db')

conn.execute("""
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS articles(
    url TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT,
    ticker TEXT,
    score INTEGER,
    summary TEXT,
    catalyst TEXT,
    risks TEXT,
    published TEXT
)
""")

conn.commit()

def get_article_text(url):
    try:
        r = requests.get(
            url,
            timeout=20,
            headers={
                "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"}
        )
        soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
        paragraphs = soup.find_all("p")
        text = "".join(p.get_text(" ",strip=True)
            for p in paragraphs
            )
        print(text)
        return text

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error fetching article text: {e}")
        return ""

def get_articles():
    articles = []

    for feed_url in RSS_FEEDS:
        feed = feedparser.parse(feed_url)
        for entry in feed.entries:
            articles.append({
                "title": entry.title,
                "link": entry.link,
                "published": getattr(entry, "published", "")
            })

    return articles

def analyse_article(text):
    try:
        prompt = f"""
        You are an investment analyst. Read the article and determine:
        1. Is this article relevant to investment decisions?
        2. Company Name
        3. Ticker if known
        4. Three sentence summary
        5. Main investment catalyst
        6. Main risk
        7 Investment score from 0 to 100
    
        Return JSON only
        Article: {text[:12000]}
        """

        response = requests.post(
            "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
            json={
                "model": OLLAMA_MODEL,
                "prompt": prompt,
                "stream": False
            }
        )

        result = response.json()["response"]
        return json.loads(result)

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error in analyse_article: {e}")
        return ""

def already_seen(url):
    cur = conn.execute(
        "SELECT 1 FROM articles WHERE url = ?",
        (url,)
    )

    return cur.fetchone() is not None

def save_article(article, analysis):
    conn.execute(
        """
        INSERT OR REPLACE INTO articles
        VALUES(?,?,?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
        """,
        (
            article["link"],
            article["title"],
            analysis["company"],
            analysis["ticker"],
            analysis["score"],
            analysis["summary"],
            analysis["catalyst"],
            analysis["risk"],
            analysis["published"]
        )
    )

def run():
    articles = get_articles()
    for article in articles:
        if already_seen(article["link"]):
            continue

        print(f"Analyzing article: {article['title']}")
        text = get_article_text(article["link"])
        analysis = analyse_article(text)

        if not analysis['relevant']:
            continue

        save_article(article, analysis)

        print(f"Saved {analysis['company']} Score={analysis['score']}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()


conn.close()
